title: Table F · the χ²-distribution
text:
The table gives the critical value (χ²)*, the boundary you compare χ² with: to its right lies probability p.









χ² has only one tail, on the right. Only a big χ² is suspicious, because then your contingency table is far from “independent” (week 4). So your whole α goes into that one tail, and the column is simply your α. No dividing by two, as with table D.

The critical value
For a two-by-two table, df = (2 − 1) × (2 − 1) = 1. Row 1, column .05: 3.84. That is the boundary from week 4: if your χ² is on it or above it, you reject the null hypothesis that the two variables are independent.


Bracketing a p
The table doesn’t give a p for every χ². But you can bracket the p between two columns.
In week 4, the phone in the bedroom gave χ² = 6.25, with df = 1. In row 1, 6.25 lies between 5.41 (column .02) and 6.63 (column .01). Then just turn the order round: a bigger χ² goes with a smaller p. So
.01<p<.02
.01 < p < .02

No times two: χ² has only one tail. Figure 1 shows it: your tail, to the right of 6.25, is smaller than the one to the right of 5.41 and bigger than the one to the right of 6.63. R gave p = .012, and that lies between them.








Figure 1: The χ²-distribution at df = 1, zoomed in on a piece of the tail. Dashed: the two table boundaries from row 1: 5.41 (column .02) and 6.63 (column .01). Your χ² = 6.25 lies between them; so the orange tail to its right is smaller than .02 and bigger than .01.





How to read it: the further to the right a stroke is, the smaller the tail behind it (the picture is zoomed in, so the orange area is really much smaller than it looks). Your stroke (6.25) is to the right of 5.41 and to the left of 6.63, so your tail is smaller than the one for column .02 and bigger than the one for column .01: .01 < p < .02. Not times two, because χ² has only one tail; even the top end, .02, is below .05, so you reject H0H_0 without knowing the exact number.
If your χ² lies beyond the last number in the row, p is even smaller than .0005. And if your df isn’t in the table, take the next smaller one that is, just as with table D.






NoteCheck in R





qchisq() gives the critical value, pchisq() the probability in the tail.

# which χ² has .05 to its right, at df = 1? In full, every argument by name:
qchisq(p = .05, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 3.841459

# the default is lower.tail = TRUE: then R uses the probability on the left. Short:
qchisq(.05, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 3.841459

# the probability to the right of your χ² = 6.25
pchisq(6.25, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 0.01241933


qchisq() gives the 3.84 from row 1, column .05, both times, and pchisq() gives your p: .012, between .01 and .02, as the table said. Forget lower.tail = FALSE, and qchisq(.05, df = 1) gives the boundary with .05 to its left: 0.0039, a completely different number.

title: Table D · the t-distribution
text:
The table gives the critical value t*t^*. To its right lies probability p: you find that at the top, in the column heading. Between −t*-t^* and t*t^* lies C: you find that at the bottom.










A split in two at the top, a split in three at the bottom
You can read table D from two sides.

At the top is a split in two: probability p in one tail, to the right of t*t^*.
At the bottom is a split in three: the middle C, with a tail on each side.

For an interval you think in splits in three, and then you look at the bottom. Both lead to the same cell: if the middle C = 95%, a probability of .95, then .05 is left over for the two tails together, and that is .025 per tail.








Figure 1: Where the t*t^* of the 95% interval from week 3 comes from, with df = 29. The blue middle is C = 95% of the t-distribution; in each orange tail, (1 − C)/2 = .025 is left over. Under the curve, a piece of table D: the column .025 (orange, one tail) and the bottom row 95% (blue, the middle) point to the same cell, 2.045.





How to read it: follow the dashed line down from t*t^*. At the top it comes out in column .025, the probability in one orange tail, and at the bottom that same column says 95%, the blue middle: two sides of the table, one cell, 2.045. One column to the left it says 1.699, under .05 and above 90%: more probability in each tail, so a boundary closer to the middle and a narrower interval.


t*t^* for an interval
In week 3 you made a 95% interval for all 30 poor sleepers, with df = 30 − 1 = 29.

At the bottom at 95%, then up to row 29: 2.045.
At the top you end up in the same column: (1 − .95)/2 = .025.

That is the t*t^* from week 3. See Figure 1.






WarningTwo-tailed with α = .05 is not the .05 column



If you test two-tailed with α = .05, you split that .05 over two tails: .025 per tail. So you look in the .025 column, or at the bottom at 95%: the same number. The .05 column belongs to one tail, and to a 90% interval.




Bracketing a p
The table doesn’t give a p for every t. But you can bracket the p between two columns.
In week 2 you found t = 2.45 for the sleep study, with df = 29. In row 29, 2.45 lies between 2.150 (column .02) and 2.462 (column .01). So:

one tail: .01 < p < .02;
two tails, times two: then p lies between .02 and .04.

Watch the order: a bigger t goes with a smaller p. Figure 2 shows why: your tail, to the right of 2.45, is smaller than the one to the right of 2.150 and bigger than the one to the right of 2.462. R gave p = .021, and that lies neatly between them.








Figure 2: The t-distribution at df = 29, zoomed in on a piece of the right tail. Dashed: the two table boundaries from row 29: 2.150 (column .02) and 2.462 (column .01). Your t = 2.45 lies between them; so the orange tail to its right is smaller than .02 and bigger than .01.





How to read it: the further to the right a stroke is, the smaller the tail behind it (the picture is zoomed in, so the orange area is really much smaller than it looks). Your stroke (2.45) is to the right of 2.150 and to the left of 2.462, so your tail is smaller than the one for column .02 and bigger than the one for column .01. Two-tailed, times two, p lies between .02 and .04: even the top end is below .05, so you reject H0H_0 without knowing the exact number.
Beyond the last column. For the paired test in week 3, t was −4.52, with df = 14. The minus sign doesn’t matter: the curve is symmetric, so look up 4.52. The biggest number in row 14 is 4.140, at .0005, and 4.52 lies even further out. So:

one tail: smaller than .0005;
two tails, times two: p < .001.

Figure 3 shows it: your stroke is beyond the last line the table knows. Table D doesn’t go further than .0005.








Figure 3: The t-distribution at df = 14, zoomed far in on the end of the right tail. Dashed: the last table boundary from row 14: 4.140, column .0005. Your |t| = 4.52, the t without its minus sign, lies even further out, so your tail (orange) is smaller than .0005: without zooming in, a hair. How much smaller, the table doesn’t say; R does, in Check in R below.





How to read it: the dashed line at 4.140 is the furthest boundary row 14 knows; to the right of it there is still .0005. Your stroke at 4.52 is even further out, so your tail is smaller than .0005. Two-tailed, times two: p < .001, well below .05, so you reject H0H_0.


If your df isn’t in the table
After 30 the table skips: 40, 50, 60, 80, 100 and 1000. If your df isn’t in it, take the next smaller one that is. For df = 44 that is 40. The same goes for a df with decimals, like the 27.95 that R gives for Welch in week 3: take 27, not 28. Without R you don’t know that 27.95; then, as in week 3, you take the lower bound, the smaller of n1−1n_1 - 1 and n2−1n_2 - 1 (here 14), and you are a little more cautious still.
Why the smaller one? The fewer degrees of freedom, the fatter the tails (week 2), and the further out t*t^* lies. At df = 40, t*t^* = 2.021; at exactly df = 44 it would be 2.015. So your interval gets a little too wide, never too narrow. And if you reject with the smaller df, R rejects with the real df as well. That is the cautious side, the same as with the lower bound for Welch in week 3.


The row z*z^*
Under row 1000 is the row z*z^*: the t-distribution with infinitely many degrees of freedom, and that is the normal distribution. That is where the three anchors from week 0 are, to three decimal places: 1.645 (column .05), 1.960 (column .025) and 2.576 (column .005). Table A doesn’t have 1.645 exactly; this row does.

title: Tables
text:
NoteWhy tables, if R can do it too?



Because then you can check yourself in more than one way. The table, R and your calculator should all come out the same; if they don’t, there is a mistake somewhere. That is how it used to be done, and we are keeping the habit: we want you to understand what is happening, not to learn a trick.
And the table shows you things R doesn’t tell you:

Why 95% and .025 belong together. In table D, 95% is at the bottom, right under the .025 column: the middle and one tail, in the same column.
Why t*t^* gets smaller as df grows. Walk down the .025 column: at df = 1 it says 12.71, at df = 29 still 2.045, and right at the bottom only the 1.960 of z. The more people, the better you know the spread, and the closer t*t^* gets to z.
What cautious testing is (the technical term is conservative). If your df isn’t in the table, you take the next smaller one: for df = 44 that is row 40, with 2.021 as the boundary. For the real df, R gives a boundary of 2.015 (that one isn’t in the table); so your boundary is a little further out. You believe H0H_0 a little longer.
What a smaller α does to your power. If you choose α = .01 instead of .05, each tail gets .005 instead of .025. In the row z*z^*, the boundary moves from 1.960 to 2.576. You reject H0H_0 less readily, even when there is a difference. So you miss such a difference more often: less power (week 5).

You don’t take a table into the exam. If a question does include a piece of a table, these pages will have shown you how to read it.


In R you type pnorm(1.5), and you have the probability to the left of z = 1.50. On paper you have the three anchors 1.645, 1.96 and 2.576 from week 0, or you look the probability up in a table.
Here are the four tables you meet most often in statistics books, in the form of Moore & McCabe’s book. The letters are that book’s letters, and there is a trap in them:

table A: the normal distribution (z);
table D: the t-distribution;
table E: the F-distribution. Watch out: F is in table E;
table F: the χ²-distribution. So table F is not the F-table.

In that book, B and C are about something else; we leave them out. Every number is calculated in R, so the table and R always say the same thing here, apart from rounding.

Look first, then look it up
Above each table is a picture with a coloured part. That part is what the table gives you. Always look at it first, because not every table is laid out the same way. Table A gives an area: everything to the left of z. The other three give a boundary, with a tail to its right that has probability p.
On a screen: tap a number, and its row and column light up. Tap it again to turn that off. On paper: put a strip of paper under the row, so you don’t slip to the wrong line by accident.


Printing
If you want to practise the way you would on paper, print them. One table per page, as at the back of a statistics book:

tables A, D and F, on four A4 pages (table A on two);
table E, on eight: the F-distribution has two kinds of degrees of freedom, and so many more numbers.

Just pressing “print” on a table page works too; then each table starts on a new page.

title: Week 6 · Assumptions and alternative tests
text:
Towards morning the whole wood was asleep.
Everyone had fallen asleep within 45 minutes, except the moth, with his phone in bed: he took 120 minutes.
“He’s spoiling my average,” said the bat, “I’m leaving him out.”
“Your average is an animal that doesn’t exist,” said the dormouse, “and he does exist.”
“And if I count him out,” the bat said at last, “he won’t have lain awake a minute less.”
He put them in a row, from early to late, with the moth at the back: not as 120 minutes but as the last one, however late that was.







What you learn this week

when you may use the bell of the z-test and the t-test
checking by eye whether your scores are skewed
transforming: pulling in a long tail with a log or a square root
working with ranks, also when two scores are equal
the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, for two independent groups
the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, for two paired measurements
the effect size r for both
what a permutation test does: understanding it, not running it yourself
in R: wilcox.test() and median()





When may you use the bell?
Remember? Statistics has no other goal than to predict and explain differences, in the population. This week you link differences in time to fall asleep to whether or not people have their phone in bed, and those times are skewed.
Since week 2 (Hypothesis tests for one mean) you haven’t been counting dots. You read your p-value off a smooth, symmetrical bell: the normal distribution for the z-test, the t-distribution for the t-test. That saves a lot of counting. But that bell is a promise, and a promise comes with conditions. Those conditions are called assumptions: things that have to hold, or the p-value is wrong.
Every test with a bell you have done so far asks for two.

Independent observations. Everyone is in the sample once, and nobody influences anyone else’s score. Children from the same class, participants who talk to each other during the study: then this condition no longer holds. For a paired test it applies to the pairs: each pair stands apart from the other pairs.
A sampling distribution that really is a bell. That is the case if the scores in the population are normally distributed. Or if your sample is big enough: then the means fall into a bell by themselves, even when the individual scores are skewed. That is the central limit theorem from week 2. In an exam this condition is called the assumption of normality.

How big is big enough? There is no fixed number for that. The more skewed the scores, the bigger the sample has to be before the means settle neatly into a bell.
With two independent groups there is traditionally one more: equal variances in both groups. The Welch version of the t-test, which R uses by default, doesn’t need it.
If the second condition doesn’t hold (the assumption is then violated), you’re stuck. The bell is then the wrong shape, and what the right shape is, you don’t know. No shape, no p-value.






TipRing the doorbell, or bang on the door



Checking assumptions is like dropping in on someone for a cup of tea. If the conditions are met, you ring the doorbell politely: you do the ordinary test.
If they aren’t, you have to get in another way. Then you bang on the door: you pick a different test, one for when the world is ugly.


What do you do when the world is ugly? Two ways out.

Transforming: converting the scores so they are less skewed, and then doing the ordinary test after all.
A test that doesn’t need a bell over your scores: a rank test (this week, the two by Wilcoxon) or a permutation test.

The tests with a bell are called parametric: they assume the population has a fixed shape that you describe with a few parameters, such as μx\mu_x and σx\sigma_x. A nonparametric test doesn’t need that shape.


Looking: is it skewed?
You check with your eyes whether your scores are normally distributed. Three things help:

a histogram: do you see a bell, or one long tail?
a boxplot: are there separate dots far away, outliers? In your head, turn it into a histogram: the tail is on the side of the separate dots.
the mean next to the median: in a symmetrical distribution they are at roughly the same place.

That last one is the quickest. A long tail pulls the mean towards it, away from where most people are. The median couldn’t care less: it simply points to the middle person, with half below and half above.






NoteThe example: time to fall asleep



A researcher asks 15 students how long it took them to fall asleep last night. Of them, eight were still on their phone in bed, and seven were not.










Figure 1: Time to fall asleep for 15 students. Blue line: the median. Orange diamond: the mean. One student with a phone lay awake for 120 minutes.





How to read it: without a phone, the diamond and the line lie close together: the mean is 13.57 minutes, the median 14. With a phone, the diamond lies far to the right of the line: the median is 29, but the mean is 39.38. That is because of one student who lay awake for 120 minutes: that student drags the mean along, but not the median.
Leave that student out, and the mean of the other seven is only 27.86.
With so few people, a histogram tells you little: a few bars, and whether that is a bell, you can’t see. Then just lay them out as dots on a line, as above.
Is this reason enough not to trust the t-test? Yes. Two small groups, and in one of them an outlier that drags the mean along. This is where you bang on the door.


Transforming: pulling in the tail

Careful: log() in R is the natural logarithm. On a calculator that is usually called ln; the log button there is a different one. Both conversions squeeze large numbers more than small ones.

Ranks: only the order counts
Say you hold three perfumes under someone’s nose and ask: how much does each one impress you, from 0 to 100? They say 20, 70 and 90. Should you take it seriously that there are exactly 50 points between the first and the second? Better not. What you do believe: the third made the biggest impression, the first the smallest.
That is the idea behind a rank test. You throw the distances away and keep only the order.

Put all the scores, from all groups together, in a row from small to large.
Give them numbers: 1, 2, 3, … Those are the ranks.
If two or more scores are equal (a tie), they all get the mean of the places they take up together.

In the example there are two students with exactly 15 minutes, one with a phone and one without. Together they take places 5 and 6, so they both get 5+62=5.5\dfrac{5 + 6}{2} = 5.5.
And that student with 120 minutes? That student simply gets rank 15, the highest. Whether that student lay awake for two hours or twenty: rank 15. So one outlier no longer carries extra weight: a rank test is robust to outliers.


The Wilcoxon rank-sum test
The Wilcoxon rank-sum test is for two independent groups. Use it when the scores are not normally distributed and the groups are small, or when your scores are only an order (ordinal). It is the alternative to the t-test for two independent groups. You will also meet it as the Mann–Whitney test: the same idea, a different name.
The hypotheses. In words:

H0H_0: neither group has systematically higher scores than the other
HaH_\text{a}: one of the two groups has systematically higher scores

In symbols, with md for the median, you write H0H_0: md1 = md2 against HaH_\text{a}: md1 ≠ md2: the medians in the two populations are equal. You may write that down: if the two distributions have the same shape, it says the same as the words above.
The idea. If there is no difference in time to fall asleep between the two groups, the ranks are mixed together at random, and each group gets its fair share. The mean rank of everyone together is N+12\dfrac{N + 1}{2}: here 15+12=8\dfrac{15 + 1}{2} = 8. If the seven students without a phone get their fair share, their ranks add up to about 7 × 8 = 56. If they come out far below that, they are systematically lower.

The Wilcoxon signed-rank test
For two paired measurements: the same people before and after, or twice under different conditions. It is the alternative to the paired t-test. Use it when the difference scores are not normally distributed and there are only a few people, or when your scores are only an order.
The name says what you do. The sign is the plus or minus of a difference: is the difference positive or negative? You first give the differences a rank without their sign, and then put the sign of each difference back on its rank: a signed rank.
The idea: pluses and minuses. You look at the difference scores. If nothing is going on, there are about as many pluses as minuses, and they are about the same size. If you see mostly pluses, and the big differences are pluses as well, then something is going on.

H0H_0: in the population, the difference scores lie above zero as often as below
HaH_\text{a}: the difference scores lie systematically above or below zero

In symbols you write H0H_0: md1 = md2 here too, just as for the rank-sum test.

The permutation test: week 1 again
Remember the dots from week 1? You pretended H0H_0 was true, made a hundred imaginary samples, and counted how many dots lay at least as far from the middle as your result. That was the p-value.
A permutation test does exactly the same. Only it doesn’t make the dots in an imaginary population, but out of your own data. No bell, no normal distribution.






NoteThe example: training or not



Eight students drew a card: four got sleep training, four didn’t. That draw will matter in a moment. By how many points did their worry score drop?

training: 9, 6, 12 and 8; mean 8.75
control: 2, 5, −1 and 3; mean 2.25

The difference in mean drop is 6.5. Real, or chance?


Suppose H0H_0 is true: the training does nothing. Then each of these eight would have had exactly the same drop, whichever card they got. And because chance decided who got which card, any other way of handing out the cards was just as likely. Then the card, training or control, means nothing. So you may shuffle the cards. That is called permuting.
Shuffling. Leave the eight drops where they are, and hand out the four training cards again among the eight people. In how many ways can you do that? In 70. For each way, work out the difference in mean drop. Each way becomes one dot (a small square in the plot below).

How to read it: the tallest stack stands above 0: eight of the 70 ways give no difference at all. At the far right, at the real difference of 6.5, there is only one square: the shuffling gives a difference that large only once in 70.
This is a sampling distribution again: this is what the difference looks like when the card means nothing. A hill around 0, as it should be.
Counting. How many dots lie at least 6.5 from 0, on both sides? Two: the real one, and its mirror image (the four biggest drops all in the control group). There are only two here because the real difference is the biggest one possible. That is often not the case, so always count. So
p=270=.029
p = \dfrac{2}{70} = .029

and .029 ≤ .05: you reject the null hypothesis that the training has no effect on worrying. Exactly as in week 1: both sides count, and the boundary itself counts too.
With bigger groups you can no longer go through all the ways. With twelve against twelve there are already 2,704,156; with the 30 people of the practice dataset, 15 against 15, already 155,117,520. Then you let the computer shuffle at random, say ten thousand times, and count among those ten thousand dots. That is called a random permutation test. The p-value then becomes a very good approximation, and it differs a tiny bit each time.
In each shuffled world you can work out any number: the difference in means, as here, but also the difference in medians. That last one, like ranks, cares little about an outlier.

You don’t need to be able to do a permutation test yourself. But you do need to understand three things:

what gets shuffled: the group names, not the scores;
what one dot is: the difference in one shuffled world, in which H0H_0 is true;
what you count: the dots that lie at least as far from 0 as the real difference, on both sides.



And the rank-sum test? Look again at the hill of rank sums in Figure 2. That was a permutation test: the group names shuffled, only over ranks instead of minutes. text:
The moth knew every burrow in the wood where a screen was still glowing at night, and in many of those burrows someone lay tossing and turning.
“Phone by the bed, bad sleep,” he said, “always together.”
“Together that often,” said the bat, “it can’t be anything else: it means something.”

title: Week 4 · Probabilities and tests for categorical variables
text:
The multiplication rule
When you see and, you quickly think of times. That’s allowed, but only with independence. You also meet this rule as the multiplicative law for independent events, or the product rule for short:






NoteMultiplication rule — only for independent variables



P(A and B)=P(A)×P(B)
P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)

Here, independent variables are two variables that tell you nothing about each other, and dependent means dependent on each other. That is not the same as the independent and the dependent variable of a study; see Three uses of independent in week 3.


Try it on the table: P(bedroom)×P(poor sleep)=.60×.40=.24P(\text{bedroom}) \times P(\text{poor sleep}) = .60 \times .40 = .24. But in the table, the joint probability is .30. The rule gives the wrong number, and that is exactly the sign that the two variables are not independent.
Why does a wrong number say dependent? You didn’t work out that .30 with a rule: you read it off the table, 30 out of 100. Reading off always works, and what you read off is right. The rule is only allowed when the two variables are independent. Here it doesn’t give what you read off. So it wasn’t allowed here: the variables are dependent. That is why you always read off first.
The rule you may always use, the general multiplicative law, has a conditional probability in it:






NoteMultiplication rule — always



P(A and B)=P(A)×P(B∣A)
P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B \mid A)



P(bedroom)×P(poor sleep∣bedroom)=.60×.50=.30P(\text{bedroom}) \times P(\text{poor sleep} \mid \text{bedroom}) = .60 \times .50 = .30. That one does work. If AA and BB are independent, then P(B∣A)P(B \mid A) is simply P(B)P(B), and the rule becomes P(A)×P(B)P(A) \times P(B). So you may always calculate with this rule. But because it always works, you can’t check anything with it: it also works when the variables are related. If you want to know whether they are independent, compare the rule for independent variables, P(A)×P(B)P(A) \times P(B), with what you read off.






NoteIf you want to go further — the addition rule





Besides and, there is or. With or you may think: at least one of the two. The phone is in the bedroom, or you sleep poorly, or both. That is different from ordering at a snack bar: fries or a burger? Then you pick one. In statistics, it may be both.
P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A and B)
P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)

You subtract that last term so that you don’t count the overlap twice. In the table:
P(bedroom or poor sleep)=.60+.40−.30=.70
P(\text{bedroom or poor sleep}) = .60 + .40 - .30 = .70

Count it yourself: 30 + 30 + 10 = 70 people have their phone in the bedroom, sleep poorly, or both. Only the 30 in the bottom-right cell are left out.
Leave out the minus, and you get .60+.40=1.00.60 + .40 = 1.00, and that is too much. The top-left cell, bedroom and poor sleep, is in both probabilities, so you count it twice. Take it off once: 1.00−.30=.701.00 - .30 = .70.
If two events don’t overlap, they are called disjoint. Sleeping poorly with the phone in the bedroom, and sleeping poorly with the phone elsewhere: both at once is impossible. The probability of both is then zero, the minus drops out, and you may simply add: .30+.10=.40.30 + .10 = .40, the probability of poor sleep. So it is still one rule.

section: In this group, or in the population?
text:
In this group, or in the population?
Look closely at what you just did. You looked at these 100 first-year students, and saw a difference: .50 against .25. For this group, that is a fact. But almost every sample shows some difference, even when the two variables are completely independent in the population. Just as in week 1, where a sample mean almost never came out at exactly 50.






TipTwo questions that look alike




“Are the variables dependent in this group?” Look only at the probabilities in the table. If the conditional probabilities are equal, then: independent. If they differ at all, however little, then: dependent, in this group. No test needed. Always work them out. With real data they almost never come out exactly equal, but in exercises and exam questions they often do. Two pairs of bars show it as well, in Figure 1: the same height, or not.








Figure 1: Left: the phone table from this week, .50 against .25. Right: no new data but a thought experiment, hence the hollow bars: the same 100 first-year students, as the table would look if phone location made no difference. Each bar is as wide as its group. The line is the probability for everyone together, 40 of the 100. On the right, exactly that share sleeps poorly in each group, so the bars end on it; on the left the line lies closer to .50 than to .25, because the wide bar counts for more.





How to read it: on the left, the height of the wide bar is the probability of sleeping poorly when your phone is in the bedroom (.50). The bar next to it is half as tall (.25): people who keep their phone elsewhere sleep poorly less often, so dependent, in this group. On the right the two bars are the same height, both .40: that is what independent looks like, and then phone location tells you nothing about your sleep.
“Are they related in the population?” or “Is the association significant?” Dependent in this group says nothing about that yet. The question then is whether the difference is bigger than chance can make it. The χ² test decides that.

title: Week 4 · Probabilities and tests for categorical variables
text:
Why 3.84: the fold
With a two-by-two table you can watch it happen. There, χ² is exactly the square of a z: the difference in the proportion of poor sleepers between the two groups, expressed in standard errors. Here 6.25=2.5\sqrt{6.25} = 2.5.
A z like that follows a smooth, symmetric bell, with a left half and a right half. A two-sided test at α = .05 means, there: .025 beyond −1.96 and .025 beyond 1.96. Square z, and the left half folds onto the right: −1.96 and 1.96 both become 1.962=3.841.96^2 = 3.84.








Figure 4: On the left, the bell of z, with .025 beyond −1.96 and .025 beyond 1.96. On the right, χ² with one degree of freedom: z squared. There the two tails of z lie together beyond 3.84: together .05, in one tail. Squaring does stretch that tail: lower and longer, but still .05.





How to read it: on the left there are two orange tails, each .025; on the right there is one, .05: in χ², the two tails of z, left and right, lie together in one tail.
That is why the critical value is 3.84, and why the ‘times two’ is already inside the right tail: the tail of z beyond 2.5 is .006, and twice that is .012, exactly the p of your χ².
Maybe you know χ² as a whale. It only gets its hump with more degrees of freedom. With one degree of freedom it is almost nothing but tail. Look again at Figure 3: at three degrees of freedom the hump is already there.





Drawn as a whale: its back is the χ² distribution with three degrees of freedom from Figure 3.

title: Week 2 · Hypothesis tests for one mean
text:
That night the bat kept track of how often everyone woke up, and he scratched it into the bark: most of them once or twice, the moth six times, a messy, lopsided list.
Then he put the animals in groups of four and scratched only the mean under each group.
Those means lay a good deal closer together, with a small hump in the middle.
“So there is a secret order in it after all,” he whispered.
“That comes of a bat taking means,” said the dormouse, “and that’s not the same thing as a secret.”
The bat looked from the messy list to the neat hump and back again, and it was still the same night.
crumbs: Week 2 · Hypothesis tests for one mean

title: Week 2 · Hypothesis tests for one mean
text:
The standard error
The second point of the central limit theorem is the most important one this week. The more people, the steadier the card. Two Einsteins in a sample of five can happen, and then the mean shoots up. Forty Einsteins in a sample of a hundred would be strange, even though it is the same share. That steadiness gets a formula of its own:
σx‾=σxn
\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \dfrac{\sigma_x}{\sqrt{n}}

Read it like this. σx\sigma_x is how far apart individual people lie. σx‾\sigma_{\bar{x}}, the standard error, is how far apart cards lie: the standard deviation of the sampling distribution. The standard deviation says how stable your data are, the standard error how stable your statistic is. Cards lie closer together than people, because a mean evens things out. How much closer? Divide by the square root of n. (If you are given the variance σx2\sigma_x^2 instead of σx\sigma_x, take the square root first.)
That it is a square root and not just n means: take four times as many people, and the bell gets not a quarter as wide but half as wide. Every extra person helps, but a little less each time. You can see it in Figure 1: from one to 4 people the width halves, from 1.22 to 0.61.






TipFour times as many, half as wide



If you want the bell half as wide, you need four times as many people. A bell a tenth as wide costs a hundred times as many people. That is why precise studies are expensive.








NoteIf you want to go further — where that square root comes from





Take σx\sigma_x = 10 and four people. If you add up their four scores, the spread of that total is not 4 × 10 = 40. High and low scores partly cancel each other out, and what adds up are the variances: 4 × 10² = 400. So the standard deviation of the total is 400=20\sqrt{400} = 20.
The mean is that total divided by 4, so its standard deviation is 20 divided by 4: 5. And that is exactly σx\sigma_x divided by 4\sqrt{4}. With n instead of 4 it goes the same way: the total has standard deviation σx\sigma_x times n\sqrt{n}, and dividing by n leaves σx\sigma_x divided by n\sqrt{n}.



Back to week 1. The worry questionnaire has σx\sigma_x = 10, and each researcher drew 25 people. Then the standard error is
σx‾=1025=105=2
\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{25}} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2

That is the width of the bell under the dots. Lay that bell over the dots of week 1, and it fits:








Figure 2: The hundred means of the worry example from week 1, with the bell that the central limit theorem predicts: middle 50, standard error 2. Each square is the mean of one sample of 25.





How to read it: above 50 stands the tallest stack, 20 squares, and above 53 there are 7: a mean of about 53 came up almost three times as rarely as one of about 50. The orange bell runs over the tops of both (at 50 it reaches 19.9 squares, at 53 it reaches 6.5), and at no stack is it a whole square off.
That it fits so precisely is no coincidence: the dots of week 1 were the counts this bell predicts. A hundred real researchers give a heap that lies just off it, with the same shape (try it in R under If you want to go further, in week 1). So you didn’t need a hundred researchers. With μx\mu_x, σx\sigma_x and n you already know how the cards lie, without drawing a single one.
crumbs: Week 2 · Hypothesis tests for one mean

title: Week 2 · Hypothesis tests for one mean
text:
One tail times two
Now the p-value: the probability of a mean at least as far from 50 as 55, if H0H_0 is true. In the bell, that is the area beyond z=2.50z = 2.50 on the right, plus beyond z=−2.50z = −2.50 on the left.








Figure 3: The sampling distribution of the worry example as a bell (middle 50, standard error 2). Orange: everything at least as far from 50 as 55 is, on either side. Each tail is .0062; together .012.





How to read it: under the axis there are two rows, the mean and below it z: every step of 2 worry points is one step in z, because the standard error is 2. The orange lines are at 45 and 55, in z at −2.50 and 2.50. The orange piece to the right of 55 is just as big as the one to the left of 45, each .0062 of the bell; together they are .012, the p-value for a mean of 55.
You don’t work out that orange area by hand; R does that. The function pnorm() gives the area to the left of a z. With a negative z you therefore get exactly the left tail:

pnorm(-2.50)

[1] 0.006209665


That is one tail: .0062, the one-tailed p-value. Two-tailed, you want both tails, and you do one tail times two:
p=2×.0062=.012
p = 2 \times .0062 = .012

Can you just do that, times two? With a bell, yes. Two-tailed is Pippi Longstocking: two pigtails. And on a bell those two tails are exactly the same size, because they lie equally far from the middle and the bell is the same on the left as on the right. So there, times two gives the same as adding up both sides, and it is quicker.
With dots you can’t count on that. The worry example of week 1 was symmetrical, because it showed the counts you can expect from a hundred researchers. The hundred drawn dots of exercise 1.5 were not, and that is why you really counted both sides there.






WarningA p above 1 does not exist



If you type pnorm(2.50) with a positive z, you get the area to the left of 2.50: almost the whole bell (.9938). Times two that is 1.9876, and a probability above 1 does not exist. You have taken the big side instead of the tail.
Two ways to get it right with a positive z: put a minus sign in front, pnorm(-2.50), or ask for the right-hand side, pnorm(2.50, lower.tail = FALSE). Both give .0062.
If you don’t want to think about the side, write 2 * pnorm(-abs(z)). abs() first turns z into a positive number, and the minus sign in front makes it negative: that way you always take a tail, whichever side z is on.
crumbs: Week 2 · Hypothesis tests for one mean

title: Week 2 · Hypothesis tests for one mean
text:
Without R: the holy z-value
In an exam you usually don’t have R. Then you are given the p-value, or you decide with the critical value: the route from week 1, now with z. (The probability for every z is also at the back, in table A.)
From now on, one number has to live in your head: 1.96. It is the only z-value you really have to know by heart, because it goes with .95 in the middle and .05 in the two tails together:








Figure 4: The standard normal distribution. Between −1.96 and 1.96 lies .95 of the bell; in each tail .025, together .05. Each p is the probability of that piece of the bell.





How to read it: in the middle piece it says p = .95: that is the area between −1.96 and 1.96, the probability that z falls there, not the height of the bell. In each orange tail it says p = .025, together .05: the α you agree on beforehand. The further out, the smaller the tails: beyond −3 and 3 there is only .003 left together.
If your z lies on or beyond 1.96 (or −1.96), then p≤.05p \leq .05 and you reject H0H_0. For the worry example: 2.50 ≥ 1.96, so you reject the null hypothesis that poor sleepers score 50 on average.
You will also come across two neighbours of 1.96, and recognising them is enough: 1.645 goes with a two-tailed p of .10, and 2.576 with .01.
You can also turn the boundaries back into worry scores: 1.96 standard errors of 2 is 3.92. The critical values are then 50 − 3.92 = 46.08 and 50 + 3.92 = 53.92. A mean on or beyond those boundaries lies in the rejection region.

title: Week 2 · Hypothesis tests for one mean
text:
Fatter tails
σx\sigma_x is one fixed number. sxs_x is not: every sample gives a different sxs_x. Sometimes it happens to be a bit small, and then your t gets bigger than it deserves. Sometimes it is a bit large, and then t gets smaller. That does not cancel out, because a test looks only at the tails, and that is exactly where the samples with too small an sxs_x end up. That extra uncertainty makes large t-values more common than large z-values. So the distribution of t has fatter tails than the standard normal distribution: the t-distribution.
How fat depends on the degrees of freedom, df for short: 𝑑𝑓=n−1\mathit{df} = n - 1. With few people, sxs_x is a wobbly estimate, and the tails are fat. With very many people you almost know σx\sigma_x, and the world behaves like z again.








Figure 5: The standard normal distribution (z) and two t-distributions. The fewer degrees of freedom, the lower the peak and the fatter the tails.





How to read it: the orange curve (t with df = 5) has a lower peak than the dark one (z). What comes off the top comes back in the tails, because the area under each curve adds up to exactly 1: out to about 1.6 on either side the orange curve lies below the other two, and beyond that above them. Beyond 1.96 and −1.96 the area under z comes to .05, under the blue t (df = 29) to .06 and under the orange one to .11: more than two times as much as under z.
More uncertainty means: you have to allow more room. Your mean has to lie further from the middle for the same p, and the critical value goes up.

The fewer degrees of freedom, the further out the boundary

NoteIf you want to go further — why n − 1?





To work out sxs_x, you first use x‾\bar{x}. And once the mean is fixed, not all n scores are free any more. If you know n − 1 of them, the last one follows from the mean: it has to make the total come out right.
Three scores with mean 10, so 30 together. The first can be anything, say 8. The second too, say 11. The third has no choice left: 30 − 8 − 11 = 11. The last person to come strolling in has no freedom; they are stuck. Of the three scores, two could move freely: n − 1 degrees of freedom.

title: Week 2 · Hypothesis tests for one mean
text:
The example: the sleep study
The practice dataset sleepstudy holds 30 first-year students who sleep badly, with their worry score before the training. Do they worry differently from the general population, where the mean is 50? You don’t know their spread, so: a t-test.
From the sample you have: x‾=54.17\bar{x} = 54.17, sx=9.31s_x = 9.31 and n=30n = 30. The six steps:

Hypotheses. H0H_0: μx\mu_x = 50; HaH_\text{a}: μx\mu_x ≠ 50; α = .05.
Sampling distribution. If H0H_0 is true, t follows a t-distribution with 𝑑𝑓=30−1=29\mathit{df} = 30 - 1 = 29.
Test statistic. First the standard error, then t:
𝑆𝐸x‾=9.3130=9.315.48=1.70
\mathit{SE}_{\bar{x}} = \dfrac{9.31}{\sqrt{30}} = \dfrac{9.31}{5.48} = 1.70

t=54.17−501.70=2.45
t = \dfrac{54.17 - 50}{1.70} = 2.45

p-value. One tail times two. The left tail comes from pt(), written out in full here:

pt(q = -2.45, df = 29, lower.tail = TRUE)

[1] 0.01027934


q is the place on the axis, df the number of degrees of freedom. lower.tail = TRUE is the default; leave it out and R picks it, and you get the area to the left of q. Short, and times two straight away: 2 * pt(-2.45, df = 29) gives p=.021p = .021. That is ≤ .05.
Statistical conclusion. Reject the null hypothesis that first-year students who sleep badly score 50 on average on the worry questionnaire.
Conclusion in context. First-year students who sleep badly worry differently, on average, from the general population; in this sample, more.

Via the critical value you arrive at the same place: 2.45 ≥ 2.05, the boundary at 29 degrees of freedom.
In a report you write the mean as M and the standard deviation as SD: the same x‾\bar{x} and sxs_x, with a different letter.


How to report it


The first-year students who sleep badly had a mean worry score that differed from the mean of 50 in the general population (M = 54.17, SD = 9.31), t(29) = 2.45, p = .021.


And with σx = 10? If you had used the σx\sigma_x of the general population after all, then z=2.28z = 2.28 and p=.022p = .022: almost the same. With 30 people, sxs_x is already a good estimate, and t looks like z. With a small group it makes much more difference; you will see that in exercise 2.4.






NoteCheck in R — the t-test by hand





R as a calculator, with the numbers of the sample:

x <- sleepstudy$worry_before
se <- sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))
t <- (mean(x) - 50) / se
t

[1] 2.451045

# two-tailed: the left tail of -t, times two
2 * pt(-abs(t), df = 29)

[1] 0.02050953


pt() does for the t-distribution what pnorm() does for the standard normal, except that it also wants to know the degrees of freedom.

title: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution
text:
Towards morning the bat was still hanging there, looking at his slip of paper — 65 on the worry questionnaire — and the longer he looked, the bigger the number grew.
“Is that a lot?” he asked quietly, because the others were asleep.
The dormouse opened one eye.
“You’re not looking, you’re worrying, and worrying is going round in circles,” she said, and the eye closed again.
The bat looked at the slip once more, and then, for the first time that night, looked away from it.
The tree was hung with animals, and each of them had a slip like that.
crumbs: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution

title: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution
text:
Step 1 · Mean
Add up all the scores and divide by n. The mean is called x‾\bar{x} (x-bar):
x‾=7+9+9+10+155=505=10
\bar{x} = \dfrac{7 + 9 + 9 + 10 + 15}{5} = \dfrac{50}{5} = 10

That is your best guess. If one of the five people walks in and you have to guess what they score, you call out 10.
crumbs: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution

title: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution
text:
Step 2 · Blue strokes
How far off were you? Subtract the mean from each score: score minus mean. Specific minus general, always in that order; then the minus or the plus takes care of itself. Each difference is a deviation, a miss. When I teach this, they are always blue strokes.








Figure 1: The blue strokes. Each stroke runs from the mean (10) to a score: −3, −1, −1 and +5, and for person 4 a 0. Above the mean plus, below it minus. Together 0.





How to read it: the stroke of person 5 is the longest (+5): with your guess of 10 you were furthest off for them, five above the mean. The one of person 1 (−3) points down and is shorter: they score three below the mean, and there you were less far off.
Add up the strokes:
(−3)+(−1)+(−1)+0+5=0
(-3) + (-1) + (-1) + 0 + 5 = 0

Always zero. The mean sits exactly where the strokes above and below cancel each other out. Handy as a check: if you don’t get zero, your mean is wrong. But as a measure of spread it’s useless: you would never miss. Those minuses have to go.
crumbs: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution

title: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution
text:
Step 3 · Squaring
Square each stroke. Squaring is literally making a square: a stroke squared is a little square, with the stroke as its side and the squared number as its area. And minus times minus is plus, so the minuses are gone.








Figure 2: Each blue stroke becomes a square. The stroke of −3 becomes a square of 9; the stroke of 0 becomes a square of 0: it counts, but you can’t see it. All the blue together is 36: that is what you add up in step 4.





How to read it: the stroke of +5 is five times as long as the one of −1, but its square is 25 times as big (25 against 1). Once squared, a long stroke counts much more heavily than a short one.






WarningThe calculator trap



Type in −3² and your calculator gives −9: it squares first and then puts the minus back in front. You mean (−3)2=9(-3)^2 = 9. Put brackets round it.
crumbs: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution

title: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution
text:
Step 4 · Adding up
Add up the squares:
9+1+1+0+25=36
9 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 25 = 36

That is the sum of squares: all the blue of the squares above, all the misses together. The further apart the scores lie, the bigger it gets.
Note the difference from step 2: the strokes always add up to 0, the squares only if everyone sits exactly on the mean. That is why you square first, then add up.
crumbs: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution

title: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution
text:
Step 5 · Dividing by n − 1
Divide the sum of squares by n − 1, here 5 − 1 = 4:
sx2=365−1=9
s_x^2 = \dfrac{36}{5 - 1} = 9

That is the variance, sx2s_x^2: the mean square. The little x says what this is the spread of: the scores x.








Figure 3: The same blue as in step 3 (36), shared out fairly over 5 − 1 = 4 equal squares: 9 each. That is the variance, the mean square. Four, because there are five people and the last one is stuck; not because you saw four squares in step 3 (the one of 0 counts too). On the same scale as the squares of step 3.





How to read it: each square is 9: smaller than the biggest one in step 3 (25) and bigger than the smallest one you saw there (1). All the blue, including that of the big square, has been shared out fairly: the variance says how big a square is on average, not how big the biggest one was.
Above all, remember: n − 1.
Why by 4 and not by 5? Because the mean is already fixed. If the five walk in one at a time, then by the last one you can do a quick calculation and know exactly what that last person scores: they have no choice left, they are stuck. Try it: the mean is 10, so together they score 5×10=505 \times 10 = 50. If you know the first four (7, 9, 9 and 10, together 35), the last one has to be 50−35=1550 - 35 = 15.
You count all five strokes, but only four of them were free to move: you don’t really have five misses but four. That is why you divide by four. In step 1 nothing was fixed yet; there you simply divide by five. That number, n − 1, is called the degrees of freedom. In round 7 you’ll do it yourself.
crumbs: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution

title: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution
text:
Step 6 · Square root
The variance is in squares: not ordinary scores any more but square scores, and nobody can picture those. The square root brings you back to ordinary strokes:
sx=9=3
s_x = \sqrt{9} = 3









Figure 4: One mean square from step 5: the variance (9) is an area. The square root gives the side: the standard deviation, 3. The thick bottom edge is a stroke again, and soon the ruler.





How to read it: the bottom edge is 3 long: the standard deviation, in ordinary scores. The 9 is the area above it, in square scores. Read that 9 as a distance, and you are saying the scores are on average 9 away from the mean: three times too far.
That is the standard deviation, sxs_x. And then always an interpretation: on average, the scores are about 3 away from the mean, to the left or to the right. Think of sxs_x as something like the mean miss: the mean length of a blue stroke.






NoteWhy not just the lengths?





Something like the mean miss, not exactly. The tempting (but wrong) feeling says: drop the minus, add up the lengths and divide by how many there are, an ordinary mean. Then you get 3+1+1+0+55=2\dfrac{3 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 5}{5} = 2 here, and not 3. That is a measure of spread too, just a different one from the standard deviation. It isn’t handy, because with squares everything that comes after just flows. So we go with the standard deviation.
That the standard deviation is bigger here is mostly down to the big square of 25: squared, the long stroke counts for much more. A little of it also comes from dividing by n − 1 instead of by n.
You can go on saying on average, the scores are about 3 away from the mean: that is how everyone says it, and about already tells you it isn’t exact.

All in a row
By hand, you put it in a table, with all the in-between answers in it. You could also type it into your calculator in one go, but I would never do that: with a table you can check back as you go. Each column is a step, and the bottom row is step 4:

Read it from the inside out: x−x‾x - \bar{x} is step 2, the square step 3, ∑\sum (adding up) step 4, the fraction step 5, the root step 6. The formula is the step card.






NoteCheck in R — is your sx right?

title: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution
text:
The step card
Remember it as a little story: the people walk in one by one, you guess the mean, and every miss is a blue stroke that turns into a square. If you can tell that story, you don’t need the formula any more.
For each step, the card says what you do, and what it means. You learn both by heart: a step you can do but don’t understand is gone again in no time.






NoteThe step card













step
what you do
what it means




1 · Mean
Add up all the scores and divide by n.
your best guess


2 · Blue strokes
Subtract the mean from each score: score minus mean.
a miss: how far off you were


3 · Squaring
Square each stroke.

title: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution
text:
Raw is rubbish
Person 5 from the example scores 15. Is that a lot?
You have no idea. 15 what? If you don’t know where the middle is, or how far apart the scores lie, 15 tells you nothing at all. Raw is rubbish: a raw score, cut off from its group, is a number without meaning. The technical name for a raw score is an unstandardised score.
But you have just worked out the middle and the spread: mean 10, standard deviation 3. Now you can do something with it.
crumbs: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution

title: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution
text:
The ruler
A z-score (the z of a single score, zxz_x; for short just z) is a count: the number of standard deviations between a score and the mean, with a minus in front if the score is below the mean. That’s all it is.
Think of the standard deviation as a little ruler, here 3 long. The z-score is the question: how many times does that ruler fit between the mean and this score?








Figure 5: The ruler is 3 long (the standard deviation), with a mark for every point. To the left, as far as the score 7, it fits exactly once: z = −1. To the right, as far as 15, it fits once completely, and then another roughly 0.67 of a ruler, the broken-off piece: together z ≈ 1.67.





How to read it: from the mean, 10, the ruler of 3 fits exactly once to the left, as far as 7: z = −1. To the right it fits once completely, as far as 13, and then roughly another 0.67, as far as 15: z ≈ 1.67. So on the right you need more rulers: 15 lies further from the mean than 7, and stands out more in this group.
z=x−x‾sx
z = \dfrac{x - \bar{x}}{s_x}

For person 5:
z=15−103≈1.67
z = \dfrac{15 - 10}{3} \approx 1.67

Just over one and a half rulers above the mean. And person 1, with 7:
z=7−103=−1
z = \dfrac{7 - 10}{3} = -1

Exactly one ruler below. The minus says: below the mean. Never forget it.
A score in rulers is technically called a standardised score, the counterpart of the raw one. That is a name, not an explanation: standardised sounds like a definition but says nothing. A tax form is standardised too.
And back. Getting from z back to the score is a short walk: start at home (the mean), and lay the ruler down z times.
x=x‾+z⋅sx=10+2⋅3=16
x = \bar{x} + z \cdot s_x = 10 + 2 \cdot 3 = 16

A z of 2 is two rulers above the middle: 16. You never need to rearrange a formula: you just set off from the middle.






NoteCheck in R — scale() is the z step





scale() does the z step for everyone at once.

# z for all five people at once
scale(x = im_fine, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)

           [,1]
[1,] -1.0000000
[2,] -0.3333333
[3,] -0.3333333
[4,]  0.0000000
[5,]  1.6666667
attr(,"scaled:center")
[1] 10
attr(,"scaled:scale")
[1] 3


At the top are the 5 z-scores, one below the other. Underneath, R shows what it calculated with: scaled:center is the mean (10) and scaled:scale the standard deviation (3). Exactly your step 1 and step 6.
That is what the two settings do: center = TRUE subtracts the mean, scale = TRUE divides by the standard deviation. These are the defaults; leave them out and R picks these: scale(im_fine) gives exactly the same. With scale = FALSE you are left with just the blue strokes.

title: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution
text:
Rule 1: draw it first
Before you calculate a single number: sketch a bell, put the middle in, put your score on the axis, and shade the piece you are looking for. It doesn’t have to be pretty; the direction has to be right.








Figure 11: This is what your sketch may look like: a bell, the middle at 50, your score 65 on the axis, and the piece to its right shaded. Wobbly is fine, as long as the direction is right. You only write the probability in once you have it; here it is already there (p = .067), so you can see where it goes.





How to read it: the line at 65 is to the right of the middle, so the shaded piece is the small side: much smaller than the white piece to its left. The probability you are after must be well under .5, and the .067 that is already there is. If you get something above .5 here, you have shaded or calculated the wrong side.
Two kinds of piece:

a split in two: one boundary, a piece on the left and a piece on the right. That goes with lower than or higher than, and you look at one tail;
a split in three: two boundaries, equally far from the middle. That goes with at least as far from the middle, on either side, and you look at two tails together.

When you later test on a bell like this, a probability from one tail is called one-tailed, and a probability from two tails together two-tailed.








Figure 12: On the left, the split in two at 65: .933 lies to the left, .067 to the right; one tail. On the right, the split in three: two tails of .067 each, together .134, and a middle of .866. Each p is the probability of that piece.





How to read it: on the left, only the piece to the right of 65 is orange: .067, the probability of a score higher than 65. On the right, the piece to the left of 35 is orange too, just as big, and together that makes .134: twice as much. If you ask for at least as far from the middle, on either side, both tails count.

title: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution
section: By hand: the rule gives a range
text:
By hand: the rule gives a range
z=1.50z = 1.50 lies between one and two rulers. To the right of z=1z = 1 lies about .16, to the right of z=2z = 2 about .025. So the tail to the right of 1.50 sits in between: smaller than .16, bigger than .025.








Figure 13: With the rule, in your head: to the right of z = 1 lies about .16, to the right of z = 2 about .025. The orange tail to the right of z = 1.50 sits in between.





How to read it: everything orange also lies to the right of the line at 1, so the orange tail is smaller than .16. And everything to the right of the line at 2 is orange too, so the tail is bigger than .025. Without calculating anything you already know: between .025 and .16.
That isn’t exact, but often it is enough: in a multiple-choice question, usually only one option falls within that range.

title: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution
section: With table A: the bell in numbers
text:
With table A: the bell in numbers
At the back is table A. For every z with two decimals, it gives the area to the left of it: the bell, but in numbers.

Look up z = 1.50: row 1.5, column .00. There you find .9332. That much of the bell lies to the left of z = 1.50.
To the right is the rest: 1 − .9332 = .0668.

That is indeed between .025 and .16, as the rule said. And in a moment pnorm() gives exactly the same.
crumbs: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution

title: Week 0 · The basics: spread, z-scores and the normal distribution
text:
Exactly: pnorm()
pnorm() gives the area to the left of a z. The first time in full, with every setting named:

# left of z = 1.5, in full: every argument by its name
pnorm(q = 1.5, mean = 0, sd = 1, lower.tail = TRUE)

[1] 0.9331928


q is the place on the axis: your z. The other three are the defaults; leave them out and R picks these. mean = 0 and sd = 1 make it the bell of z, and lower.tail = TRUE means: the lower tail, on the left. R puts 0.9331928 on your screen for it, rounded .933. If you want the right-hand side, you set lower.tail = FALSE: not the lower one, you want the upper one.








Figure 14: Which tail pnorm() gives, sketched by hand at z = 1.50. On the left the default, lower.tail = TRUE: the area to the left. On the right lower.tail = FALSE: the area to the right.





How to read it: in the left bell everything to the left of 1.50 is hatched, almost the whole bell: .933. That is what you get if you say nothing about the tail. In the right one only the narrow piece to the right of 1.50: .067. If you are after the narrow piece of your sketch and R gives you something above .5, you have the wrong side: check that lower.tail = FALSE is there.
Short, the way you will usually type it:

# left of z = 1.5: the big side of the split in two
pnorm(1.5)

[1] 0.9331928

# right of it: the small side
pnorm(1.5, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 0.0668072


Left .933, right .067. Those two add up to 1, because together they are the whole bell. Indeed between .025 and .16: about 7 in 100 people score higher than 65.
So without mean and sd, pnorm() calculates in the bell of z itself: mean 0, standard deviation 1. That bell is called the standard normal distribution, N(0,1)N(0, 1). How to make R calculate on the scale of your own questionnaire is in In R: probabilities from the bell.
The split in three. How many people score at least as far from 50 as 65, on either side? Equally far on the other side is 35, at z = −1.50. The bell is symmetrical, so the tail to the left of 35 is exactly as big as the one to the right of 65. Two tails together, so one tail times two:
2×.067=.134
2 \times .067 = .134


# two tails: the right tail, times two
2 * pnorm(1.5, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 0.1336144

# or the left tail of -1.5, times two: the same
2 * pnorm(-1.5)

[1] 0.1336144


That times two is allowed here, because a smooth bell is exactly the same size on both sides. A dot plot, as in week 1, looks like such a bell but is never exactly symmetrical; there you really count both sides.

The three anchors
Three values of z keep coming back. After a few weeks you’ll know them without trying:

The three anchors of the normal distribution








z

outside ±z (two tails together)
between −z and z

Figure 15: The three anchors. To the right of 1.645 lies .05 (one tail). Beyond ±1.96 lies .025 on each side, together .05. Beyond ±2.576, .005 on each side, together .01.





How to read it: on the left and in the middle there is the same amount of orange, .05 in total. On the left it sits in one tail, which starts at 1.645. In the middle it is split over two tails, .025 each, and then you have to go further out, to 1.96. On the right there is even less orange, .005 per tail, and that only starts at 2.576.
1.96 is the holy z-value. By the rule of thumb, .95 lies within two rulers; more precisely, it lies within 1.96. At 1.96 there is .025 in each tail, together .05.
1.645 is the other holy z-value, and it often gets mixed up with the first. At 1.645 there is .05 in one tail. Draw it, and you’ll see.
In testing, the anchors are called critical z-values.
Reasoning with the anchors. You can place any z between the anchors. But look at your drawing first: one tail or two?

One tail. Our z=1.50z = 1.50 lies below 1.645, so to the right of it lies more than .05. Right: pnorm() gives, rounded, .067.
Two tails together. A z of 2.40 lies between 1.96 and 2.576. Further out than 1.96, so together less than .05. Not as far as 2.576, so together more than .01.

You don’t have an exact number, but you do have enough to decide.






NoteRound 5 — from memory: from variance to anchor



On a questionnaire about self-acceptance (how gentle are you with yourself when something goes wrong?), scores in the population are normally distributed. The mean is 30 and the variance is 25. Someone scores 38.

What is that person’s z-score?
Are they in the highest .05? Use only an anchor.

z=38−305=1.60
z = \dfrac{38 - 30}{5} = 1.60

Anyone who divides by 25 instead of by 5 gets 0.32: far too small.
The highest .05 starts at the first anchor, 1.645. Their 1.60 lies just below it, so to the right of it lies just a little more than .05. This person is only just outside it.
In R, pnorm(1.6, lower.tail = FALSE) gives the area to the right: .055.

title: Inferential Statistics Practice Book
text:
Week 0 (the basics) and weeks 1 to 7 are in English.




What this practice book is
A practice book for inferential statistics: from sample to population, and from a difference to a decision. Not a summary, and not a second textbook, but a place where you do it.
The order is always the same. By hand first: you count, calculate and draw it yourself, because only then do you see what is happening. Then R, as a check: R does the same calculations again, and you see that they come out right. The other way round doesn’t work. If all you know is which buttons to press, you don’t know what comes out.


What a week looks like

The material, with one example you work through step by step.
A check in R, in a box you click open.
The week in R: what you do in R yourself that week, out in the open on the page.
Practice: exercises with a worked answer that you open once you have had a go yourself. For calculation exercises there is a short answer first, with the full worked answer below it.
An exam block: questions the way you will meet them in an exam — multiple choice with four options, a number to fill in, or yes or no.

Week 1 is the coat rack. It doesn’t go deep, but it puts up all the hooks the other six weeks will hang on. Whatever week 1 promises a later week is worked out in that week.






NoteTables, alongside R



After week 7 there are tables for z, t, F and χ², like the ones in Moore & McCabe’s book. You don’t take a table into the exam; the tables are there because we want you to understand what R calculates, and to be able to check yourself in more than one way: the table, R and your calculator should all come out the same.




How to read the symbols
A symbol appears in this book in three ways, and that is on purpose:

in an explanation, the word, with the symbol next to it the first time: the population mean (μx\mu_x);
in a calculation, the maths, as on your scrap paper: p=2100p = \dfrac{2}{100};
in a sentence you copy into a report, the way APA writes it: p = .012 — no zero before the point, and three decimals below .100.

We write probabilities as probabilities (.05), not as percentages (5%). The decimal separator is a point, not a comma.

Where R comes in, you work with the practice dataset sleepstudy.RData: thirty students in their first year who sleep badly, half of them with sleep training and half without. The numbers are made up, and chosen so that the same table can carry three tests in later weeks.

It was already getting light when the bat came home, and now he knew for sure.
“Poor sleepers worry more than other animals,” he said to the dormouse, who woke up because he said it.

text:
The other route: the critical value
You can also draw a boundary in the dot plot beforehand. Which means are so far from 50 that the p-value drops below .05?








How Far From 50 Does a Mean Have to Lie to Be Significant?


distance from 50

From a distance of 5 on, p drops below .05. So the boundaries are 45 and 55: those are the critical values. Everything on or beyond those boundaries is the rejection region — so 55 itself belongs to it. If your x‾\bar{x} falls in that region, you reject H0H_0.








Figure 4: The critical values 45 and 55 (dashed lines). The rejection region is everything on or beyond those lines.





How to read it: the right-hand line runs through the stack at 55: that one square lies on the boundary, so it belongs to the rejection region. The stack at 54 (3 squares) stands just inside the line: here, at a mean of 54, you do not reject H0H_0, even though the difference is only one point.
It’s like a fever. From 38 degrees on, you have a fever; that 38 is a critical value, agreed on before anyone put the thermometer in. The lines themselves are the critical values; everything on and beyond the lines is the rejection region. In an exam, those two are a favourite mix-up.
Two routes, the same decision:

the p-value route — count both sides, and set that p next to α = .05;
the critical-value route — draw the boundaries beforehand, and see whether x‾\bar{x} lies on or beyond a boundary.

They always come out the same. What goes wrong is switching halfway: setting a p from only one side next to .05, for example. Pick one route per exercise and see it through.






NoteIf you want to go further — why the boundaries shift a little in week 2





The means in the dot plot are rounded to whole numbers. So “53 or higher” counts everything from 52.5 up. That is why counting dots gives a rough p, and rough boundaries.
In week 2 you work out the same example exactly, without rounding. Then the p at 53 is not .22 but .13, and the boundaries are not at 45 and 55 but at 46.08 and 53.92. You can look up the p at 53 yourself, at z = 1.50 in table A, or have R calculate it; both give .13. At a mean of exactly 54, the decision even flips: counting says .08, calculating says .046.
That is not a fault of the dots. That is how a picture of a hundred rounded numbers works: it shows the shape, not the third decimal.

A report from your script
With one command you turn a script into a report: your code, with the output and the figures underneath, in one HTML file. It looks like the R part above. In RStudio: File > Compile Report… (or Ctrl+Shift+K, on a Mac Cmd+Shift+K), and choose HTML. The report appears next to your script, with the same name.
Compile Report runs your whole script again, from top to bottom, and starts with an empty Environment. If something is in your Environment only because you typed it in the console, the report doesn’t know about it: it only knows what is in your script. If it doesn’t work, check four things:

are your script and your data in the same project folder?
are library() and load() at the top of your script, before the lines that need them?
is there a View() or install.packages() in it? Take them out: they belong in the console.
does your script itself stop with an error somewhere? Run it from top to bottom first (Code > Run Region > Run All); where it stops there, the report stops too.

text:
After the sleep training the bat hung above the lake and looked sourly at the moth, who was fluttering carefree around the reeds.
“I still worry more than he does,” he said.
“He always worries less, that takes no training, just being a moth,” said the dormouse, “you’d do better to compare yourself with a bat.”
The bat looked down, and in the still water hung a bat, the right way up, looking back at him.
“Then from now on I’ll hang next to myself,” he said, “the one from before the training next to the one from now.”
He looked at the water once more and chuckled: “At least then I’ve got someone who worries exactly the way I do.”

text:
The hypotheses
Under H0H_0 nothing changes, on average. Then you expect a mean difference of zero: bread at the baker’s. Not exactly zero in every sample, because chance always shifts things a little, but in the population, yes.

H0H_0: μd=0\mu_d = 0 — on average, poor sleepers who do the training worry as much after as before
HaH_\text{a}: μd≠0\mu_d \neq 0 — on average, something changes

μd\mu_d is the mean difference in the population: Greek, because that is a number you don’t know. You’ll also come across it as δ (delta).
crumbs: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals

title: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals
text:
The test






NoteThe paired t-test



t=d‾−0𝑆𝐸d‾=d‾sdndf=n−1
t = \dfrac{\bar{d} - 0}{\mathit{SE}_{\bar{d}}} = \dfrac{\bar{d}}{\dfrac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}}}
\qquad df = n - 1

With n the number of pairs: the number of difference scores, not the number of measurements.


That is the t-test for one mean from week 2, on the column of differences, with μ₀ = 0.
Is −3.467 a lot? You can’t tell. Raw is rubbish: a difference of three points can be big or small, depending on how much chance shifts things around. So you ask: how many times does the standard error, the ruler, fit into that difference?
First the ruler:
𝑆𝐸d‾=sdn=2.97315=2.9733.873=0.7676
\mathit{SE}_{\bar{d}} = \dfrac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}} = \dfrac{2.973}{\sqrt{15}}
= \dfrac{2.973}{3.873} = 0.7676

Keep those four decimals until the end. Then divide:
t=−3.4670.7676=−4.52df=15−1=14
t = \dfrac{-3.467}{0.7676} = -4.52
\qquad df = 15 - 1 = 14

The ruler fits into it more than four times, downwards: the difference is negative. You get the two-tailed p-value from the t-distribution, just as in week 2: one tail, times two. That is allowed because the t-distribution is symmetric; the other tail is exactly as heavy.

2 * pt(-4.52, df = 14)

[1] 0.0004804551


That is p < .001. (Further down, R calculates with the unrounded t and gets 0.0004839: the same, apart from the rounding of t.) In an exam you are given a p like that. If you want to see for yourself where it lies, bracket it in table D. In row 14, the last column is the column .0005, and the number there is 4.140; your |t| = 4.52 lies beyond even that. So one tail holds less than .0005, and the two tails together less than .001: p < .001, just as in R.
Deciding. p ≤ .05, so you reject the null hypothesis that poor sleepers who do the training worry as much after as before, on average: that is your statistical conclusion. In plain words, your conclusion in context: after the training the participants worry differently, on average, from before; in this sample their scores are 3.47 points lower.






NoteHow to write it up



The participants’ worry scores differed between before and after the training, t(14) = −4.52, p < .001; afterwards their scores were on average 3.47 points lower.








WarningDoes that mean the training works?



This test doesn’t tell you that yet. It compares after with before, in the same people. But worry can also go down without any training: the exam week is over, or whoever scored extra high at the first measurement scores a bit lower the second time all by itself. To judge the training you need a group that got no training. That comes at the end of this week, in So does the training work?.








NoteCheck in R — the paired t-test





In R you can do it in two ways, and they give exactly the same result. How you select the training group is in week 1, in In R: choosing rows.

training <- sleepstudy[sleepstudy$group == "training", ]

# 1. the two columns, and tell R that they are paired
t.test(training$worry_after, training$worry_before, paired = TRUE)


    Paired t-test

data:  training$worry_after and training$worry_before
t = -4.5163, df = 14, p-value = 0.0004839
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -5.113000 -1.820333
sample estimates:
mean difference 
      -3.466667 

# 2. first the difference scores, then the test for one mean against 0
training$difference <- training$worry_after - training$worry_before
t.test(training$difference, mu = 0)


    One Sample t-test

data:  training$difference
t = -4.5163, df = 14, p-value = 0.0004839
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -5.113000 -1.820333
sample estimates:
mean of x 
-3.466667 


Both give t = −4.5163, df = 14, just as by hand. The interval at the bottom is the same too; what that is comes in The confidence interval.

section: The standard error of a difference
crumbs: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals

title: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals
text:
The test






NoteThe independent t-test (Welch)



t=(x‾1−x‾2)−(μ1−μ2)𝑆𝐸x‾1−x‾2=x‾1−x‾2s12n1+s22n2
t = \dfrac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - (\mu_1 - \mu_2)}{\mathit{SE}_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}}
= \dfrac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}

R works out the degrees of freedom; see Welch, pooled and Levene.


Why does μ1−μ2\mu_1 - \mu_2 drop out? Because you calculate in the world of H0H_0, just as in week 1. There μ1−μ2\mu_1 - \mu_2 is zero, and subtracting zero does nothing.
t=51.267−52.5333.3867=−1.2663.3867=−0.37
t = \dfrac{51.267 - 52.533}{3.3867}
= \dfrac{-1.266}{3.3867} = -0.37

The ruler here is 3.3867 points, and the difference isn’t even half a ruler. R gives df = 27.95 with it, and then p = .71.
Deciding. p > .05, so you do not reject the null hypothesis that both groups worry equally on average afterwards. Afterwards, no difference between the groups has been shown. That is not the same as “the groups worry equally”: see week 1.






NoteHow to write it up



Afterwards, worry scores did not differ significantly between the training group and the control group, t(27.95) = −0.37, p = .71.








TipWhy paired is so much more sensitive



Take the training group again, with the same difference of −3.47. Now pretend that before and after are two separate groups, and work out the ruler from this section:

as two separate groups: 3.4982, because people differ a lot from one another (the standard deviation is 9.69 before and 9.47 after);
as pairs: 0.7676, because each person is compared with themselves (sds_d is only 2.97).

Same people, same difference, and a ruler more than four times as long. As separate groups p = .33; as pairs p < .001.
Someone who worries a lot worries a lot before and after. In the difference per person that drops out; between two separate groups it stays, and a small difference drowns in it. You can see it in Figure 1 too: the dots run from 37 to 72, but they all lie close to the line.








NoteCheck in R — the independent t-test






# one column of scores, and after the tilde (~) the column with the group
t.test(sleepstudy$worry_after ~ sleepstudy$group,
       alternative = "two.sided", mu = 0, var.equal = FALSE, conf.level = 0.95)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  sleepstudy$worry_after by sleepstudy$group
t = 0.37401, df = 27.951, p-value = 0.7112
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group control and group training is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -5.671257  8.204590
sample estimates:
 mean in group control mean in group training 
              52.53333               51.26667 


Look at the sign. R says t = 0.37, you calculated t = −0.37. R subtracts the groups in the order they come in, and that is alphabetical: first control, then training. So R calculates control minus training, and you calculated training minus control. Same test, same df, same p; only the sign flips, and the interval is mirrored with it.
The second line has four arguments by name. These are the defaults; leave them out and R picks these: two-tailed (alternative = "two.sided"), a difference of 0 under H0H_0 (mu = 0), each group keeps its own spread (var.equal = FALSE) and a 95% interval (conf.level = 0.95). var.equal = FALSE is Welch’s test, the one you use in this book; that is why the top says Welch Two Sample t-test. So the short version gives exactly the same: t.test(sleepstudy$worry_after ~ sleepstudy$group, var.equal = FALSE). In this book you always keep that one argument, so you can see which test you are running.
