title: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals
text:
Back to the poor sleepers
The worry example from week 1: a questionnaire with σx\sigma_x = 10, and a sample of 25 poor sleepers. The standard error is then 1025=2\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{25}} = 2. Suppose you find x‾\bar{x} = 53.
Your best guess for μx\mu_x is 53: the point estimate. But you know that 53 may be off, because a sample mean shifts. So you put a margin around it: so many standard errors to the left, and so many to the right. For 95%, that is 1.96 of them.






NoteThe interval for μx\mu_x, when you know σx\sigma_x



x‾±z*⋅σxn
\bar{x} \pm z^* \cdot \dfrac{\sigma_x}{\sqrt{n}}

z*z^* (z-star) is the number of standard errors you walk: 1.645 for 90%, 1.96 for 95%, 2.576 for 99%. Those three are best simply known by heart. z*z^* is the critical value from week 1, now as a number of standard errors; you’ll also see it written as zα/2z_{\alpha/2}. The part z*⋅σx/nz^* \cdot \sigma_x / \sqrt{n} is called the margin of error: how far you go to the left and to the right.


53±1.96×2=53±3.92so from 49.08 to 56.92
53 \pm 1.96 \times 2 = 53 \pm 3.92
\quad \text{so from } 49.08 \text{ to } 56.92

That is the 95% confidence interval: [49.08, 56.92]. Does 50 lie in it? Yes. A population with μx\mu_x = 50 fits these data just fine, and that is why you do not reject H0H_0: μx\mu_x = 50. The dots in week 1 said so too, and so did the z-test in week 2.
And with x‾\bar{x} = 55? Then the interval runs from 51.08 to 58.92. Now 50 is not in it: you reject the null hypothesis that μx\mu_x = 50.
crumbs: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals

title: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals
section: When you don’t know σx: t
text:
When you don’t know σx: t
Usually you don’t know σx\sigma_x, and you fill in the standard deviation sxs_x from your sample. Then you don’t walk z*z^* standard errors but t*t^*, from the t-distribution with df=n−1df = n - 1. That one is a little bigger: if you are estimating rather than knowing, everything gets a little wider.






NoteThe interval for μx\mu_x, with t



x‾±t*⋅sxndf=n−1
\bar{x} \pm t^* \cdot \dfrac{s_x}{\sqrt{n}} \qquad df = n - 1

t*t^* is the critical t-value; you’ll also see it written as tα/2(df)t_{\alpha/2}(df).


Take all 30 poor sleepers from the sleep study, and their worry score before the training: x‾\bar{x} = 54.167, sxs_x = 9.311.
𝑆𝐸x‾=9.31130=9.3115.477=1.700t*=2.045(df=29)
\mathit{SE}_{\bar{x}} = \dfrac{9.311}{\sqrt{30}}
= \dfrac{9.311}{5.477} = 1.700
\qquad t^* = 2.045 \;\; (df = 29)

54.167±2.045×1.700=54.167±3.477
54.167 \pm 2.045 \times 1.700
= 54.167 \pm 3.477

The interval is [50.69, 57.64]. Fifty lies just outside it. With z*z^* = 1.96 you would have got [50.83, 57.50]: a little narrower, and that is precisely too narrow, because you didn’t know σx\sigma_x.
You can see where that t*t^* lies in Figure 2: it is the boundary where .025 of the t-distribution is still left to the right, and just as much to the left of −t*-t^*. Together .05 outside, .95 in between.








Figure 2: The t-distribution with df = 29. Between −2.045 and 2.045 lies .95; in each orange tail, .025. t*t^* = 2.045 is the boundary of the right tail.





How to read it: the two orange tails are mirror images of each other, and that is why in the interval above you walk equally far to each side: 2.045 standard errors.
You get t*t^* in R with qt(). In full, with every argument by name:

qt(p = 0.025, df = 29, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 2.04523


You ask for the t-value with .025 still above it on the right (p = 0.025): half of the .05 that falls outside the 95% interval. That right is in lower.tail = FALSE: not the left tail (the lower tail), but the right one. The default is lower.tail = TRUE: leave that argument out and R counts the probability from the left, so qt(p = 0.025, df = 29) gives −2.045, the boundary of the left tail. So the short version works too, with the probability from the left: qt(0.975, df = 29) gives the same 2.045.
Without R, you look up t*t^* in table D: row df = 29, and 95% at the bottom. The picture there shows why that is the same cell as the column .025.
crumbs: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals

title: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals
text:
What 95% means: the horseshoe
This is the hardest part of the week.
Throw a horseshoe at a post. Sometimes the post ends up between its arms, sometimes not. An interval is a horseshoe like that, and μx\mu_x is the post: it stands still, and you don’t know where. The 95% belongs to the throwing: if you draw a sample very many times and make an interval like this each time, 95 out of 100 intervals catch μx\mu_x. Drawing very many times like that is called repeated sampling.








Figure 3: Twenty samples of 25 poor sleepers, from a population in which μx\mu_x = 50 (the grey line). Each bar is the 95% interval of one sample; the square on it is that sample’s mean. All the bars are the same length, because σx\sigma_x and n are fixed; only their middle shifts. Of the 20 bars, 19 catch μx\mu_x; the orange bar misses.





How to read it: of the 20 squares, 19 lie between 46.08 and 53.92, less than half a bar from μx\mu_x (3.92, the same margin as with x‾\bar{x} = 53 above), and their bars reach the grey line. Only the orange square lies outside, at 56.17, and its bar does not reach it. Over very many samples, 95% of the squares lie that close to μx\mu_x, and that is why 95% of the bars hit.
In Figure 3 you know μx\mu_x, because the samples are invented. That exactly one misses is chance, in these twenty: the next series may miss none, or three. Only over very many series does it become one in twenty. In real research you throw once, and you don’t see the post. You only know that your way of throwing hits in 95% of cases.






NoteWhat a 95% confidence interval means



If you draw a sample very many times and make an interval like this each time, then 95% of those intervals contain the true μx\mu_x.


In plain words you say: “with 95% confidence, μx\mu_x lies between 49.08 and 56.92”. The word confidence does the work there: it says something about the method, the throwing. About this one interval there is no probability left to state; it catches μx\mu_x, or it doesn’t.
So in a multiple-choice question you pick the repeated-sampling reading (“if you draw very many times … then 95% of the intervals contain μx\mu_x”), if it is among the options. You’ll also meet it in a shorter form, as “the range in which μx\mu_x lies in 95% of cases”. That is the same reading: “the cases” are the repeated samples.






WarningThree readings that are wrong




“95% of poor sleepers score between 49.08 and 56.92.” Wrong: the interval is about the mean μx\mu_x, not about individual people. Individual scores spread much more widely than means (week 1: the scores of one sample next to the sampling distribution).
“There is a 95% probability that x‾\bar{x} lies in the interval.” Wrong: x‾\bar{x} is the middle of the interval. It always lies in it.
“There is a 95% probability that μx\mu_x lies in this interval.” Strictly speaking, no: μx\mu_x stands still, and this one horseshoe lies around it or it doesn’t. The 95% belongs to the throwing. If the repeated-sampling reading is among the options, that is the right answer.

title: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals
section: Interval and test say the same thing
text:
Interval and test say the same thing
You already saw it with 53 and 55. It always holds, as long as interval and test calculate in the same way (the same standard error, both with z or both with t) and you test two-tailed:

if μ₀ lies in the 95% interval, then p > .05 and you do not reject H0H_0;
if μ₀ lies outside the 95% interval, then p ≤ .05 and you reject H0H_0.

A 99% interval goes with α = .01, a 90% interval with α = .10. The interval gives you something extra for free: roughly how big the difference is.
crumbs: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals

title: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals
text:
Wider or narrower
Three dials set how wide an interval is. All three are in the formula x‾±z*⋅σx/n\bar{x} \pm z^* \cdot \sigma_x / \sqrt{n}:

The confidence level (z*z^*). If you want to be surer, you throw a wider horseshoe.
The sample size (n). A bigger n makes the standard error smaller, and the interval narrower. It goes with the square root: four times as many people gives an interval half as wide.
The spread (σx\sigma_x, or sxs_x). The more the scores differ, the wider.

The first dial for the poor sleepers, with x‾\bar{x} = 53:

The same mean, three confidence levels


confidence level
z*z^*
interval
width




90%
1.645
[49.71, 56.29]
6.58


95%
1.96
[49.08, 56.92]
7.84


99%
2.576
[47.85, 58.15]
10.30



The confidence level is also called the coverage: what share of the horseshoes hit.

title: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals
text:
The interval for a difference
The same recipe works for this week’s two tests. You put the margin around the difference you found, and look whether 0 lies in it.






NoteIntervals for a difference



Paired, with df=n−1df = n - 1:
d‾±t*⋅sdn
\bar{d} \pm t^* \cdot \dfrac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}}

Independent, with Welch’s df:
(x‾1−x‾2)±t*⋅s12n1+s22n2
(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) \pm t^* \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2}}



Paired, the training group. t*t^* = 2.145 with df = 14, and the ruler was 0.7676:
−3.467±2.145×0.7676=−3.467±1.647
-3.467 \pm 2.145 \times 0.7676
= -3.467 \pm 1.647

The interval is [−5.11, −1.82]. Zero is not in it, just as the test said. And you can see straight away roughly how big the drop is: drops of 1.82 to 5.11 points fit these data.
Independent, training against control. t*t^* = 2.0486 with df = 27.95:
−1.266±2.0486×3.3867=−1.266±6.938
-1.266 \pm 2.0486 \times 3.3867
= -1.266 \pm 6.938

The interval is [−8.20, 5.67]. Zero is in it. And look how wide it is: afterwards the training group may score 8.20 points lower on worry than the control group, but also 5.67 points higher. Not significant here mainly means: these data don’t know yet.






NoteHow to write up an interval



From before to after the training, worry scores changed by −3.47 points on average, 95% CI [−5.11, −1.82].








NoteCheck in R — the intervals





t.test() always gives you the 95% interval as well, under 95 percent confidence interval. You ask for another level with conf.level, and you get just the limits out with $conf.int:

# the 95% interval for μₓ, worry before, all 30
t.test(sleepstudy$worry_before)$conf.int

[1] 50.68987 57.64346
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

# the paired interval for the training group, now 90%
t.test(training$worry_after, training$worry_before, paired = TRUE,
       conf.level = 0.90)$conf.int

[1] -4.818644 -2.114689
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.9


The 90% interval is narrower than the 95% interval [−5.11, −1.82]: less sure, so a narrower horseshoe.

title: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals
section: Paired: two columns side by side
text:
Paired: two columns side by side

## The training group ----
training <- sleepstudy[sleepstudy$group == "training", ]

A boxplot of the two columns side by side:

boxplot(training$worry_before, training$worry_after, names = c("before", "after"),
        ylab = "worry score")







Figure 4: Worry before and after in the training group (n = 15). The median drops from 54 to 51.





How to read it: the thick line in each box is the median; it drops from 54 to 51. The boxes themselves, the middle half of the scores, are both 10.5 points tall: after, people are spread just as far apart as before. Next to that height, a drop of 3 points is small, and the two boxes largely overlap.
That boxplot doesn’t see the pairs: it puts two groups next to each other. For paired data a scatterplot says more. Each point is one person, and the line abline(a = 0, b = 1) is where after is exactly equal to before (a = 0: the line starts at zero; b = 1: one step up for every step to the side):

plot(training$worry_before, training$worry_after,
     xlab = "worry score before", ylab = "worry score after")
abline(a = 0, b = 1)







Figure 5: Worry before against after in the training group, with the line after = before.





How to read it: a point below the line is someone who worries less after than before. There are 12 below it, 2 exactly on it and only 1 above it, and that one point (before 54, after 55) worries only 1 point more after. So almost everyone goes down, and the boxplot above didn’t show that: it only put two groups next to each other.
Then the test:

## The paired test ----
t.test(training$worry_after, training$worry_before, paired = TRUE)


    Paired t-test

data:  training$worry_after and training$worry_before
t = -4.5163, df = 14, p-value = 0.0004839
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -5.113000 -1.820333
sample estimates:
mean difference 
      -3.466667 


Note the order: worry_after first, then worry_before. R calculates the first minus the second.
And how are those differences spread? Make the column, and a histogram:

training$difference <- training$worry_after - training$worry_before
hist(training$difference, main = "", xlab = "difference (after minus before)", ylab = "count")







Figure 6: The 15 difference scores (after minus before) of the training group, from −9 to 1.





How to read it: the tallest bar, from −6 to −4, counts 6 people; the only bar to the right of zero, from 0 to 2, counts 1. So almost everyone worries less after: 12 of the 15, because the bar from −2 to 0 also counts the 2 people with a difference of exactly 0 (R puts a number on a boundary in the bar to its left).
The paired test assumes that the differences in the population are roughly normally distributed. When that matters, and what you do if it isn’t so, comes in week 6 (Assumptions and alternative tests).






WarningDon’t forget paired = TRUE



Without paired = TRUE, R thinks you have two separate groups, and it does a Welch test. With these data:

t.test(training$worry_after, training$worry_before, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value

[1] 0.3301853


p = .33 instead of less than .001. No error message, no warning: just a different answer. It is exactly the calculation from Why paired is so much more sensitive: without the pairs, R counts the differences between people again.

section: Independent: one column of scores, one column for the group
text:
Independent: one column of scores, one column for the group

## Two groups ----
# left of the tilde (~) the scores, right of it the group
boxplot(sleepstudy$worry_after ~ sleepstudy$group, xlab = "group", ylab = "worry score after")
t.test(sleepstudy$worry_after ~ sleepstudy$group, var.equal = FALSE)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  sleepstudy$worry_after by sleepstudy$group
t = 0.37401, df = 27.951, p-value = 0.7112
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group control and group training is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -5.671257  8.204590
sample estimates:
 mean in group control mean in group training 
              52.53333               51.26667 








Figure 7: Worry afterwards, per group (15 in control, 15 in training). The medians: 56 and 51.





How to read it: the box for training (47 to 57.5) lies entirely inside the box for control (44 to 58.5). The medians do differ by 5 points (56 against 51), but the median of control sits high in its box: the lower half of that group is stretched out, and that pulls the mean down. So the means, which the test looks at, differ by only 1.27 (52.53 against 51.27, at the bottom of the output), and the test finds no difference: p = .71.
Type the tilde yourself. If you copy it from a PDF, it is often a different character that only looks the same, and you get an error message.

title: Week 3 · Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals
text:
Asking for the interval

## Another level, and only the limits ----
t_out <- t.test(sleepstudy$worry_after ~ sleepstudy$group, var.equal = FALSE, conf.level = 0.99)
t_out$conf.int

[1] -8.092912 10.626245
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.99


t_out is what comes out of the test. With t_out$ you can also ask for $statistic (t), $parameter (df) and $p.value. R calls the degrees of freedom a parameter of the t-distribution. Type ?t.test and look under Value for the whole list.

title: Week 5 · Effect sizes and power
text:
The bat had finished his report on the sleep training, and at the bottom, underlined twice, it said: worrying has fallen significantly.
He read it again and nodded.
“A little, or a lot?” asked the dormouse, who had been woken by the nodding.
“Significantly,” said the bat, and heard himself say it.
“A little, or a lot?” asked the dormouse once more, and was asleep again.
The bat looked at his underlined word, and it didn’t say either.

title: Week 5 · Effect sizes and power
section: Which standard deviation do you divide by?
text:
Which standard deviation do you divide by?
With one mean that’s clear: the standard deviation of the scores (σ if you know it, as here; otherwise s of the sample). With two groups and with paired measurements you have a choice, and both choices can be defended.

Whichever you take: say which. Two researchers who divide the same data differently get a different d, and both have calculated correctly.
If an exercise doesn’t say which, then with two groups take the s of the control group (or the pooled s if there is no control group), and with paired measurements the s of the pre-test. Those are the easiest choices to interpret; the reasons are below.

The mean of the difference scores is often written as d‾\bar{d} (d-bar). That is not Cohen’s d: d‾\bar{d} is a difference in points, Cohen’s d a difference in standard deviations. You’ll also see Cohen’s d with a hat, d̂\hat{d}: an estimate from the sample.

Two groups: training versus control
You know the practice dataset sleepstudy from week 1: 30 students in their first year who sleep badly; half of them got sleep training. Everyone’s worrying was measured, before and after. For each person, take the drop: worry score before minus worry score after. Does worrying drop more in the training group than in the control group?

The difference is 3.47 − 1.07 = 2.40 points. Two choices for the standard deviation:

The control group. It shows how much people without training differ from each other in their drop. Then you’re saying: this is how big the effect of the training on the drop is, measured against the ordinary noise.
d=2.404.76=0.50

The pooled s: the two groups together. With two groups of equal size, that’s the square root of the mean of the two variances:
sp=s12+s222=2.972+4.7622=8.82+22.662=3.97
s_\text{p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{s_1^2 + s_2^2}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2.97^2 + 4.76^2}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{8.82 + 22.66}{2}} = 3.97

And then, just as above:
d=2.403.97=0.60

Both medium: the training group drops by roughly half a standard deviation more.
And now the test. Welch gives t(23.49) = 1.66, p = .11. Not significant. A medium difference, and yet you don’t reject the null hypothesis that the drop is, on average, the same size in both groups. That looks contradictory. Hold on to it for a moment; at the end of this week, with power, it falls into place.

title: Week 5 · Effect sizes and power
section: Paired: the training group before and after
text:
Paired: the training group before and after
Now look only at the 15 people in the training group. Before the training their mean worry score was 54.73, afterwards 51.27: a drop of 3.47 points. The paired t-test says t(14) = 4.52, p < .001. Highly significant: a drop like that would be very rare if nothing were going on. But how big is that drop?

Divided by s of the pre-test (9.69): how much people differed from each other in worrying before the training.
d=3.479.69=0.36
d = \dfrac{3.47}{9.69} = 0.36

Small: for d, that means 0.20 or more, but under 0.50.
Divided by s of the difference scores (2.97, the s of the drop in the table above): how much the drops differ from one another.
d=3.472.97=1.17
d = \dfrac{3.47}{2.97} = 1.17

Large: for d, that means 0.80 or more.

Small and large, from the same data. Both say something true:

Compared with how much people differ from each other in worrying (before the training, one scored 37 and another 72), a drop of 3.47 points is small.
But almost everyone in the training group worries a little less (12 of the 15 go down; two stay the same and one goes up by one point), and the drops are much alike. Compared with how much those drops differ from one another, the drop is large: it is very consistent.

If you want to know whether the effect of the training on worrying matters in daily life, the pre-test is the handiest one to divide by. You need the difference scores when you work out the power of a paired test; software does that for you. Always say which one you took.






Tipd doesn’t grow with n; t does



If you divide by the s of the difference scores, d looks just like the test statistic t:
d=mean differencesdifferencet=mean differencesdifferencen
d = \dfrac{\text{mean difference}}{s_\text{difference}}
\qquad
t = \dfrac{\text{mean difference}}{\dfrac{s_\text{difference}}{\sqrt{n}}}

The only difference is the n\sqrt{n}. So t=d×nt = d \times \sqrt{n}. Here: 1.166×15=4.521.166 \times \sqrt{15} = 4.52. (Take d to three decimals: with 1.17 the rounding gives you a slightly different t.)
More people make t larger (and p smaller), but not d. That’s exactly why you put d next to it: the effect size is only about size.

title: Week 5 · Effect sizes and power
text:
Two worlds: God and Allah
Power is easiest to grasp with two worlds on one number line. Here, God and Allah stand for two hypotheses that cannot both be true.

God says: poor sleepers just score 50 on average. That is the world of H0H_0. That’s the world you did your test in, in weeks 1 and 2.
Allah says: no, they score 55 on average. That is the world of one particular alternative. Careful: in week 1, 55 was the mean of your sample (x‾\bar{x}); here it’s the mean of the whole population (μx\mu_x), in Allah’s world.

The worry example again: σx\sigma_x = 10, n = 25, so a standard error of 2, and a two-tailed test with α = .05. Calculated rather than counted, the critical values lie at 50±1.96×250 \pm 1.96 \times 2, so 46.08 and 53.92. (Counting dots in week 1, you got 45 and 55; calculated, the boundaries lie slightly closer to the middle.) You set those boundaries in God’s world. But you can also lay them over Allah’s world, and see how often you reject H0H_0 there.








Figure 1: Two worlds on one number line. Top: the world of H0H_0 (μx\mu_x = 50). Bottom, mirrored: the world of one particular alternative (μx\mu_x = 55). The dashed lines are the critical values 46.08 and 53.92. Orange: α, false alarm. Purple: β, missed. Green: power.





How to read it: top and bottom have the same two dashed boundaries, but they cut off very different pieces. Of God’s hill, only a thin orange rim lies beyond the boundaries, .05 together. Of Allah’s hill, the green part lies beyond the right-hand boundary, and it is larger than the purple part between them: if the real world is at 55, you reject H0H_0 more often than not.
Now one world at a time, from top to bottom.

God’s world (top). The orange tails beyond the boundaries together make α = .05: that’s how often you reject H0H_0 while H0H_0 is true. A false alarm: a Type I error.
Allah’s world (bottom). The same boundaries, a different hill. If a sample mean falls between the boundaries, you don’t reject H0H_0, while Allah’s world is the real one: that’s the purple part, β. If it falls beyond a boundary, you rightly reject H0H_0: the green part, the power.

Working out the power. How often does a sample mean in Allah’s world fall beyond 53.92? Turn that boundary into a z inside Allah’s hill:
z=53.92−552=−0.54
z = \dfrac{53.92 - 55}{2} = -0.54

In the figure you can already roughly see the answer: the green part is well over half of Allah’s hill. You can get it exactly in two ways.
With R as a calculator: 1 - pnorm(-0.54) gives the probability to the right of z=−0.54z = -0.54, .705.
With Table A: at z=−0.54z = -0.54 the table gives .2946, the probability to the left. So the probability to the right is 1 − .2946 = .7054: to three decimals, the same .705. Power is an area, just like every probability in Table A.
In an exam, a probability like that is given in the question.
The little piece to the left of 46.08 counts too, because there you also reject H0H_0. But it lies so far from 55 that it is smaller than .001. So:
power=.71β=1−.71=.29
\text{power} = .71
\qquad
\beta = 1 - .71 = .29

If poor sleepers really score 55 on average, then with 25 people you see it in about 7 out of 10 studies. In the other 3 you miss it. The difference of 5 points is a d of 0.50: medium.






NoteCheck in R — the power with pnorm()





pnorm(z) gives the probability to the left of z. So the probability to the right is 1 - pnorm(z).

# the critical boundary on the right: 50 + 1.96 times the standard error
boundary <- 50 + 1.96 * 2

.705, and with the negligible piece on the left added and rounded, .71.

More people make the standard error smaller. The two hills get narrower, overlap less, and the power goes up.
A larger real difference (a larger d) pushes Allah’s hill further away from God’s. Less overlap, more power. You usually don’t have your hand on that knob: reality decides how large the difference is.
A larger α (the significance level) moves the boundaries inward: more power. But also more false alarms. So a stricter α (.01) costs power.
Less spread (measuring more precisely) also makes the hills narrower. Note: then d gets larger too, because you divide the same difference by a smaller σ.

A larger sample gives more power, but not more Type I errors. If H0H_0 is true, you reject H0H_0 in at most a fraction α of studies, however large your n. What a huge sample does do: make tiny differences significant. That’s the real warning, and you knew it already from the table at the top of this week.

title: Week 5 · Effect sizes and power
section: How many people do you need?
text:
How many people do you need?
You work out power before the study, in a power analysis. You choose the smallest difference you want to be able to see, and look for the sample that sees it with power .80: in 8 out of 10 studies. Which difference? The smallest one that matters in practice, or what earlier research found. If you know nothing, you often take Cohen’s medium d = 0.50.
Software draws that as a power curve. Below, for the test you learned in week 3: two independent groups of equal size.








Figure 2: Power of the t-test for two equal-sized, independent groups, two-tailed, α = .05, at three effect sizes. The dashed line is power .80.





How to read it: a point on a line is the power with that many participants, if the real effect is as large as that line’s. At 90 participants the middle line (d = 0.50) is between .6 and .7, the bottom one (d = 0.20) between .1 and .2; calculated, that is .65 and .16. So with the same number of people, you see a medium effect more than four times as often as a small one.
Read off where a line crosses the dashed line at .80. Reading off gives a round number; calculated (with R) it’s exact:

for a large effect (d = 0.80) you need 52 participants, 26 per group;
for a medium effect (d = 0.50), 128, so 64 per group;
for a small effect (d = 0.20) you don’t come close even with 200: there you’re at .29. Calculated, you need 788, far outside the figure.

That’s how expensive a small effect is.






NoteIf you want to go further — working out the sample size for one mean





For the z-test for one mean you can find the n by hand. At power .80, the two peaks of God and Allah lie exactly 1.96 + 0.84 standard errors apart: 1.96 from God to the boundary (that’s what goes with α = .05, two-tailed), and 0.84 from the boundary to Allah. Why 0.84? If the boundary lies 0.84 standard errors to the left of Allah’s peak, then .80 of Allah’s hill lies to the right of the boundary: exactly the power you want. In R you find it with qnorm(.80): the z with .80 to its left, and because the hill is symmetric that’s the same distance. (That’s how you find 1.96 with qnorm(.975).) Without R, both are in Table D, in the row z*z^*: column .025 and column .20. Expressed in d:
n=(1.96+0.84d)2
n = \left( \dfrac{1.96 + 0.84}{d} \right)^2

For the worry example, with d = 0.50:
n=(1.96+0.840.50)2=31.36
n = \left( \dfrac{1.96 + 0.84}{0.50} \right)^2 = 31.36

Always round up: 32 people. With 31 you just miss the .80 (.795), with 32 you make it (.807).

title: Week 5 · Effect sizes and power
text:
Not significant: now what?
Back to the sleep study. The difference in drop between the groups was medium, and yet not significant (p = .11). You now know why that’s no riddle.
Suppose the training really has a medium effect on the drop in worrying: d = 0.50. What was the probability, then, that this study, with 15 people per group, would see it? Read it off at 30 participants in the power curve, or work it out: power = .26. A study like this misses a medium effect in about 3 out of 4 cases.
So this p-value says little. The difference may well be there; the study was too small to see it. That’s what week 1 meant by not significant is not the same as equal, now with a number attached. For a power of .80 you would have needed 64 people per group.






WarningYou work out power beforehand



Above it says suppose d = 0.50. That’s Cohen’s benchmark for medium, chosen the way you would choose it beforehand. The sleep study, with the s of the control group, happened to come out at 0.50 as well, but that is not why this value was chosen. If you work out the power afterwards with the d you happened to find, you learn nothing new: a non-significant result then always gives a low power. It’s your p-value in disguise.

title: Week 5 · Effect sizes and power
text:
Too few and too many
A study with too little power is a bet you’ve half lost before you start. The sleep study showed it: even if the training really works, a study like that only sees it in .26 of cases. And then the report says “no significant difference”, and someone reads that as “the training doesn’t work”. All 30 participants took part for an answer that was never likely to come.
You can have too many, too. Measure a great many people and even a difference that doesn’t matter in daily life comes out significant (exam question 1 below shows one). And all those people gave their time for a question that far fewer could have answered.
That’s why you work out the power beforehand, and always put an effect size next to your p.






NoteIf you want to go further — simulating power in R





Power is a probability over a great many studies. In R you can simply do those studies: draw thousands of samples of 25, work out the z-test for each one and keep its p-value.
First in God’s world (H0H_0 true, μx\mu_x = 50):

set.seed(5)

# one study: 25 people, mean, z, p
one_p <- function(mu) {
  scores <- rnorm(25, mean = mu, sd = 10)
  z <- (mean(scores) - 50) / (10 / sqrt(25))
  2 * pnorm(-abs(z))
}

p_god <- replicate(5000, one_p(mu = 50))
hist(p_god, breaks = seq(0, 1, by = .1), main = "", ylab = "count",
     xlab = expression(italic(p)), xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = seq(0, 1, by = .2), labels = c("0", ".2", ".4", ".6", ".8", "1"))

# how often do you reject H0 when H0 is true?
mean(p_god <= .05)

[1] 0.0468








Figure 3: Five thousand p-values when H0H_0 is true.





How to read it: all the bars are about the same height. The bar from 0 to .1 counts 474 of the 5,000 studies, the one from .9 to 1 counts 509: if H0H_0 is true, a high p turns up just as often as a low one.
So a high p-value is no sign that H0H_0 is right. And you reject H0H_0 in about .05 of the studies: that’s α, the false alarm.
Then in Allah’s world (μx\mu_x = 55):

p_allah <- replicate(5000, one_p(mu = 55))
hist(p_allah, breaks = seq(0, 1, by = .1), main = "", ylab = "count",
     xlab = expression(italic(p)), xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = seq(0, 1, by = .2), labels = c("0", ".2", ".4", ".6", ".8", "1"))

# how often do you reject H0, now that the alternative is true? That is the power.
mean(p_allah <= .05)

[1] 0.7098








Figure 4: Five thousand p-values when μx\mu_x = 55.





How to read it: the bar from 0 to .1 now counts 4,036 of the 5,000 studies, the bar next to it only 423: the first is almost ten times as tall. In God’s world that same first bar counted 474. So in Allah’s world a study usually gives a small p, and how often it comes out at or below .05 is the power.
Now you reject H0H_0 in about .71 of the studies: the .71 you worked out by hand, give or take chance. That way you can find the power of any test, even a test for which there is no formula.

title: Week 7 · Choosing a test, and an overview
text:
At the end of the winter there were seven little coats hanging at the entrance to the tree, one for every kind of weather, and the bat hung beside them and could not work it out.
“One that fits all weathers,” he said, “there must be one.”
The dormouse, who had not worried about a thing all winter, woke up and looked not at the coats but outside.
“Look at the weather first,” she said.
Outside, a thin rain was falling, the first of the spring.
They went on watching it together, one just awake, the other awake all winter.

title: Week 7 · Choosing a test, and an overview
section: The row: what do you measure?
text:
The row: what do you measure?
Look at the outcome. It is one of three kinds, and the three are themselves in order: with each next one you know a little more about your scores. Such a kind is called a level of measurement; in brackets, each time, is what that level is called.

A category (nominal) — yes or no, a degree programme, a living situation. All you know is that the boxes differ from each other. So you count: how many people are in each box?
A rank order (ordinal) — four smileys (‘really bad’, ‘bad’, ‘good’, ‘really good’), or ‘poor, fair, good, very good’. Boxes again, but now the order is fixed: put them on a number line and ‘bad’ always comes before ‘good’. Exactly where, you don’t know: from ‘bad’ to ‘good’ isn’t necessarily as far as from ‘good’ to ‘really good’. A mean pretends all the steps are the same height, so a mean is not something you calculate here. So you rank: higher or lower, not how much higher.
A number with fixed distances (interval or ratio), also called numerical — a score, a time, an age. Now you also know how far: from 20 to 30 minutes is just as far as from 30 to 40. So you calculate: a mean, a difference.

If you count, you have two categorical variables: your outcome, and usually the group someone is in (training or control, or three degree programmes). Those groups are made up of different people. That is why the χ²-test for independence sits in the column two groups, different people, even with more than two groups.
The χ²-test compares what you count in each box with what you would expect if the two variables had nothing to do with each other. It doesn’t need the bell, only enough people per box: the expected frequencies mustn’t be too small. That is week 4 (Probabilities and tests for categorical variables).
You can also count a rank order in boxes (that is why week 4 calls it categorical too), but then you throw the order away. A rank test keeps it.
Watch out for numbers that are a code. If it says ‘1 = at home, 2 = in student housing, 3 = other’, that is a category. A 3 isn’t more ‘living’ than a 1. A mean living situation of 1.8 means nothing. If it says ‘1 = poor, 2 = fair, 3 = good’, it is a rank order: the digits give the order, not the distance.

title: Week 7 · Choosing a test, and an overview
section: The column: who are you comparing with whom?
text:
The column: who are you comparing with whom?
There are three possibilities: the three columns.

One group against a fixed number. You have one sample and a number to set it against: the mean in the general population, a norm, an old value. These are the one-sample tests from week 2 (Hypothesis tests for one mean), so only for a number: you don’t take the mean of a rank order.
Two groups with different people in them. Training versus control, smokers versus non-smokers. Whoever is in one group isn’t in the other: the samples are independent.
The same people, measured twice. Before and after, morning and evening. The samples are paired. That also goes for pairs that belong together, such as the two halves of a pair of twins or of a couple.

Two groups, independent or paired, are both week 3 (Hypothesis tests for two means and confidence intervals). If you are torn between the two, ask this question: can you link each score to exactly one other score? Yes: paired. No: independent.
Your data file gives it away too. If the two measurements sit side by side on one row — a column before and a column after — it is paired. If there is a column that says which group someone is in, and one column with the outcome, it is independent.
With paired measurements you work out the difference for each person. Then you have one set of difference scores, and you test that against 0. So a paired test is really a test for one mean: the mean difference. Only, the σd\sigma_d of such difference scores is in no test manual anywhere. That is why with paired measurements you don’t ask about σd\sigma_d, but whether the bell is OK.
crumbs: Week 7 · Choosing a test, and an overview

title: Week 7 · Choosing a test, and an overview
section: With a number: do you know σx, and is the bell OK?
text:
With a number: do you know σx, and is the bell OK?
With one group the question is: do you know the standard deviation of the population (σx\sigma_x)? It is sometimes in the manual of a questionnaire. If you know it, the z-test. If you don’t, and you estimate it with the standard deviation of your sample (sxs_x), the t-test, with n − 1 degrees of freedom. How big your group is doesn’t decide it here: even with a hundred people it is the t-test if you don’t know σx\sigma_x.
With two groups and with paired measurements the question is: is the bell OK? In an exam that is called the assumption of normality.
The t-tests use a bell-shaped sampling distribution. That is allowed if the scores in the population are roughly normally distributed; with paired measurements, it is about the difference scores.
Note the word population. No sample is exactly normally distributed, and that isn’t the question either. The question is whether your scores could come from a roughly normally distributed population. You check that with your eyes: a histogram, a boxplot or a dot plot, and the mean next to the median.








Figure 1: The drop in worry score per person, on the left in the training group, on the right in the control group. One dot is one person. On the left the dots lie close together; on the right one lies far away, at −11.





How to read it: the further right a dot is, the more that person’s worrying dropped. On the left the lowest dot is at −1, only one point from the next one (0); on the right the orange dot, the outlier, is at −11, seven points from the next one (−4). A gap like that in a group of 15 is why you have doubts on the right about whether the bell is OK, and not on the left: that one person pulls the mean of the control group down, from 1.93 without them to 1.07 with them.
The bell is not OK if:

your outcome is a rank order: the distances between the steps aren’t fixed;
your groups are small and the scores are clearly skewed, or there is a big outlier in them.

How big is big enough? There is no fixed number for that. There is a direction: with a handful of people per group it has to look neat; with dozens per group the bell is less fussy, because then the sampling distribution of the mean becomes bell-shaped by itself, even if the scores are skewed. That is the central limit theorem from week 2.
In between you sometimes have doubts, as on the right in Figure 1: 15 people and one big outlier. In doubt, do both. If the t-test and the rank test give the same decision, your conclusion doesn’t hang on the bell. Do say which one you take first, and why.
If an exercise says nothing about the shape of the scores, the bell is OK.
If the bell isn’t OK, you take a rank test: the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with two independent groups, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test with paired measurements. They first put the scores in order (with paired measurements: the differences) and calculate with the ranks. An outlier there is simply ‘the highest’, however far away it lies. That is week 6 (Assumptions and alternative tests), and there a rank test is also called a non-parametric test.
These are the names you’ll meet in an exam: the rank-sum test and the signed-rank test. In JASP the rank-sum test is called Mann-Whitney.






NoteIf you want to go further — one group without the bell





The t-test for one group leans on the bell too. Still, the table has no rank test for one group against a fixed number. There is one: the signed-rank test can also set the scores of one group against a fixed number, instead of against a second measurement. In this practice book you only use it for paired measurements. So with one group you only check whether there is anything odd in your scores, and you say so.

title: Week 7 · Choosing a test, and an overview
text:
What goes with every test
The six steps of week 1 stay, whichever test you choose. What differs per test is in steps 2 and 3: which sampling distribution, and which test statistic. On top of that come three things you didn’t have yet in week 1.

The six steps, and what comes on top






step from week 1
what you write down for every test




1. hypotheses
H0H_0 and HaH_\text{a}, two-tailed, even if the researcher expects a direction; and α (.05)


2. sampling distribution
which one: z, t with how many degrees of freedom, χ², or the ranks


3. test statistic
the number from your sample: z, t, χ², W or T⁺


4. p-value
the p from R, next to α; or the test statistic next to a boundary such as 1.96


5. statistical conclusion
reject H0H_0 or not, and which H0H_0


6. conclusion in context
the answer to the research question, in plain words


on top: the interval
which values your data still allow (week 3)


on top: the effect size
how big the difference is (week 5)


on top: a figure
a bar chart with χ², a boxplot per group with two groups, a histogram of the difference scores with paired measurements









TipAnd the permutation test?



It isn’t in the table, because you don’t carry it out by hand. You do need to know the idea, and you already know it. Shuffle the group labels, work out the difference between the groups, and do that very many times. Every shuffled difference is a dot: that is what the difference looks like when the group doesn’t matter. Then count how many dots lie at least as far from 0 as your real difference.
That is exactly what you did in week 1 with the cards, only here the dots are made by shuffling instead of by imaginary samples.
